2080119,ca.proc.d.1960-12-02.5.1.2,1960-12-02,0daa460f-b2c1-447e-abbe-c4bd1f237b32,ca.m.6630,Mr. Hazen Argue (Assiniboia):,,NOVA SCOTIA,REPORTED CLOSING OF COLLIERIES,,I should like to direct a question to the Prime Minister. In view of reports that a number of collieries in Nova Scotia are to be shut down, can the Prime Minister say whether arrangements have been made for a meeting between the Dominion Coal Company and the federal government to the end that these mines may be kept open?

,Co-operative Commonwealth Federation (C.C.F.),,Hazen Robert Argue,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=0daa460f-b2c1-447e-abbe-c4bd1f237b32&Language=E&Section=ALL

Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):,Prime Minister,NOVA SCOTIA,REPORTED CLOSING OF COLLIERIES,,No such meeting has been arranged as yet. However, continual discussions have been going on in connection with representations which have been received from the areas in question. I think it was some 10 days ago that a meeting took place in Ottawa at which the whole matter was carefully reviewed not only by the representatives from Cape Breton but by representatives of the company and the ministers concerned.

,Progressive Conservative,,John George Diefenbaker,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=84909dc1-9a60-44b3-a939-2393ab563089&Language=E&Section=ALL

Herridge (Kootenay West):,,FINANCE,USE OF IMPORTED CAR BY GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA,,Yesterday, Mr. Speaker, you ruled a question by me out of order as being concerned with a person's private affairs, and as I was not sure of my ground I resumed my seat. Now I have had reliable information, and I wish to rephrase my question. In view of the fact that the Bank of Canada has purchased a car for Mr. Coyne in the United States and is now in the process of purchasing an even more luxurious one, would the Minister of Finance inform the house whether this is government policy?

,Co-operative Commonwealth Federation (C.C.F.),,Herbert Wilfred Herridge,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=b815a117-7953-4900-b152-afc56dfc44a1&Language=E&Section=ALL
2080130,ca.proc.d.1960-12-02.7.1.3,1960-12-02,5b04fb13-968f-4dac-80f6-3b569378e120,ca.m.5224,Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):,Minister of Finance and Receiver General,FINANCE,USE OF IMPORTED CAR BY GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA,,I think the hon. member must be aware from the form of his own question that government policy is not involved in this-situation in any way. The Bank of Canada is not responsible to the government. The Bank of Canada is responsible to parliament, and the government has no control whatever over the internal operations of the Bank of Canada.

,Progressive Conservative,,Donald Methuen Fleming,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=5b04fb13-968f-4dac-80f6-3b569378e120&Language=E&Section=ALL
2080131,ca.proc.d.1960-12-02.7.1.4,1960-12-02,b815a117-7953-4900-b152-afc56dfc44a1,ca.m.5560,Mr. Herridge:,,FINANCE,USE OF IMPORTED CAR BY GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA,,A supplementary question. Does the minister agree with the purchase by the Bank of Canada of these automobiles in the United States?

,Co-operative Commonwealth Federation (C.C.F.),,Herbert Wilfred Herridge,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=b815a117-7953-4900-b152-afc56dfc44a1&Language=E&Section=ALL

reports regarding a summit meeting of the communist leaders of the world being held in Moscow?

,Progressive Conservative,,Harry Oliver White,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=ed7c9721-7803-4bd8-a892-696cdd38f5a0&Language=E&Section=ALL
2080142,ca.proc.d.1960-12-02.9.1.1.3,1960-12-02,84909dc1-9a60-44b3-a939-2393ab563089,ca.m.3212,Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):,Prime Minister,EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,REPORTED MEETING OF COMMUNIST,LEADERS,As the house knows, a meeting of the leaders of communist parties has taken place in Moscow and has been going on for some three weeks. A short communique was issued. It reveals nothing about what progress if any has been made toward bringing about a compromise in the dispute between the U.S.S.R. and communist China.

All I can say is that we will have to await further developments before endeavouring to assess the meeting or its effects on that dispute, which of course, has very significant and important implications for western relations with the communist countries.

,Progressive Conservative,,John George Diefenbaker,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=84909dc1-9a60-44b3-a939-2393ab563089&Language=E&Section=ALL

Can the Prime Minister say whether the Canadian communist party was represented at this meeting?

,Liberal,,Louis-Joseph-Lucien Cardin,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=93651988-2631-417c-96e4-174904755eb1&Language=E&Section=ALL
2080144,ca.proc.d.1960-12-02.9.1.1.5,1960-12-02,84909dc1-9a60-44b3-a939-2393ab563089,ca.m.3212,Mr. Diefenbaker:,Prime Minister,EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,REPORTED MEETING OF COMMUNIST,LEADERS,I cannot say that in answer to the hon. gentleman. All I know is that there were 81 communist parties represented. Whether the Canadian communist party on this occasion fell behind in its usual position in that regard, I cannot say.

,Progressive Conservative,,John George Diefenbaker,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=84909dc1-9a60-44b3-a939-2393ab563089&Language=E&Section=ALL

2080168,ca.proc.d.1960-12-02.12.7,1960-12-02,d3117809-e7d1-45d2-9762-d1a2621aa271,ca.m.3975,Mr. Speaker:,Speaker of the House of Commons,PROVISION FOR CONTINUANCE OF RAILWAY OPERATIONS,,,Before putting the motion I must determine whether there is a prima facie question of privilege, and I shall be glad to hear hon. members on that point. A motion based on privilege must be founded on a finding by the Chair that there is a question of privilege. I think there is a proper question of privilege in that if, as is asserted and as appears to be the case, the Hansard report of the final stages of the proceedings of the committee is incorrect, that is a matter that the house will be concerned with as a breach of its privilege to have its proceedings correctly reported.

However, the consequences which the hon. member for Skeena suggests do not appear to me to be self-evident, because what in fact ensued was that the chairman reported the bill as amended and the house itself adopted the report of the committee which was a report of the amended bill without reservation or limitation. If there was an irregularity in the proceedings of the committee that irregularity, it seems to me, is cured by the action of the house itself. Therefore the suggestion made by the hon. member for Skeena appears to me, without opportunity for further reflection, not to follow from the omission which was made in committee.

On the other hand, the incorrect report in Hansard is a matter which I think the house very properly has a duty to take into account. Whether the hon. member, in view of what I have said, wishes me to proceed with this motion is a matter for him to decide.

Our position is that in compelling the men to remain at work, the bill should also compel the companies to pay wages that a conciliation board, with a chairman appointed by the government, found to be fair and reasonable.

We believe therefore, Mr. Speaker, that clause 3 should have been amended to vary the collective agreements in order to bring them into conformity with the recommendations of the Milvain conciliation board. If the government had accepted that change in the bill, which we have already proposed, we of course would have voted for third reading of this bill with the amendment.

This would have assured overwhelming, perhaps even unanimous, parliamentary approval for legislation to prevent a threatened railway strike. However, if the government persists in maintaining the bill as it is, we cannot vote to force men to work for wages judged to be substandard by the Milvain conciliation board set up by the government. Therefore the government and its supporters will have to take exclusive responsibility for this unjust method to prevent a strike, which strike, however, we also believe must be prevented at this time in the public interest.

2080187,ca.proc.d.1960-12-02.12.26,1960-12-02,9fa12394-384b-4e7a-872b-8230b0e27dd7,ca.m.3489,Mr. Harold E. Winch (Vancouver East):,,PROVISION FOR CONTINUANCE OF RAILWAY OPERATIONS,,,Mr. Speaker, on this occasion of third reading of this very important bill I would like to say a few words and take a few minutes' time on behalf of our group in this House of Commons.

We recognize very completely the importance and seriousness of the problem which is facing this country and this house, and the difficulties that arise. We recognize- and all hon. members have stated this- the effect that a cessation of work in the transportation industry could have, not only on those directly involved but those who would be indirectly affected as Canadian citizens engaged in other operations in our Canadian economy.

A great deal has been said both pro and con in these last few days on the legislation which is now before us. 1 think the position of our group has been made exceedingly clear. We regret that matters should have come to a position where the introduction of such legislation was deemed necessary by the government. We have pointed out that in our opinion, had there not been delayed action by the government it should have been possible, among responsible government, responsible employers and responsible employees, to work out a satisfactory solution. We feel most strongly-and we have demonstrated this by word and by vote up to this time-that in the introduction of the legislation the government has not taken what we consider a fair approach or an unbiased attitude. We in this group, sir, cannot accept in principle the introduction of legislation which will remove from a segment of the workers of this country an inalienable right ^yaXan ky law and given to most, because of the failure of government, employers and employees to work out a satisfactory solution.

Very briefly, we feel it is wrong. We cannot endorse the removal of a right, in particular in an industry which is very strongly regulated by government, when there is a majority report and when it must be admitted by all fair men upon due consideration that the 110,000 employees affected now have a gap, I believe, of around 29 cents an hour compared with the standard which has been generally accepted; that is, compared with those employed in the durable goods industries.
We feel that on almost every ground of principle affecting the rights of these workers, their positions and their standards, the government is really remiss in the manner in
which the legislation has been introduced_______
or should I say in what is left out of the legislation as far as the employees are concerned.

The government is asking, through the medium of this legislation, for the removal of what should be inalienable rights. As the law is going to be amended at this time, these rights will be removed. These employees, having carried on in a responsible manner now for over a year, are being asked

Maintenance of Railway Operation Act to continue tor another six months with no change in their standards and with no remedial action to close the gap between the standards which have been accepted for many years. In particular, Mr. Speaker, we cannot see how, with the passage of this legislation there will be a different position on May 15 of next year. In other words, we are going to have a continuous period of anxiety for just over six months, and then perhaps we will have to face the identical situation which we are facing at the present time.

We think that is unfortunate. There is nothing in the legislation, and nothing has been said by the government, that can possibly lead us to any conclusion other than that this is merely a policy-wise move, a stall, hoping that something may happen in the next six months. The Prime Minister stated what will most likely occur before May 1; that is, a lifting of the freight rate freeze, which I think undoubtedly must involve the question of whether there will be a continuation of the subsidy as far as freight rates are concerned. That is a situation, sir, which is almost untenable when you look at it today and try to look forward to what the situation will be on May 15. It is these reasons, amplified in the two days' discussion, that we felt had to be mentioned on the motion for third reading of this bill.

But, Mr. Speaker, there is one point that disturbs us greatly and it is this. As the legislation now stands-definitely as the legislation now stands-and considering anything expressed by the Prime Minister or the Minister of Labour, there is nothing to indicate that there will be any differentiation between now and six months from now. This can only lead to what I term a period of anxiety for the employees directly or indirectly affected. We feel that something should be placed in the legislation itself which would indicate that there was a possibility of removing the cause of this anxiety in the next six months, that this should not be left to wishful thinking on the part of the Prime Minister or the Minister of Labour with the probability that we shall be facing a situation on May 15 similar to the one we are facing at the present time. In other words, we feel there should be some provision in the legislation to direct that between now and May 15, when this bill becomes inoperative, there shall be a continuation of negotiations.

We feel that both men and industry must be reasonable. I know that workers are reasonable, because few things are so unpleasant as being out of work. The Canadian economy, as well as the position in which the workers find themselves, demand the removal

of this period of six month's anxiety leading to a likely repetition of the present situation six or seven months from now. Although I personally regret very much the necessity of placing in legislation any provision to insist that responsible men should get together,

I do not feel, because of the importance of this question to the country's economy and to the workers involved, that we can afford to leave the situation up in the air. It is simply not good enough to rely on wishful thinking.
It is because we feel that this question is of major importance that I move, seconded by the hon. member for Skeena:
That Bill No. C-45 be not now read a third time but that it be referred back to the committee of the whole house for the purpose of reconsidering clause 3.

May I say in this regard that I should like to have mentioned more fully the purpose I have in mind, but there are certain rules of procedure; some things are in order and others are out of order. I know this is in order. I want the house to understand that the purpose of this amendment on third reading is to get the bill back into committee of the whole on clause 3 in order that the committee might give consideration to whether we should not give a legislative indication to the companies and to the employees that there is not to be a hiatus between now and May 15, and that the parties must get together as responsible people in an effort to work out a collective agreement before the expiry of a bill which is to become an act of parliament.

May I end by saying that we in this group are moving this amendment because we feel it is our responsibility as members of parliament to do so in the interests of the Canadian economy and of the Canadian workers who are directly or indirectly affected.

2080216,ca.proc.d.1960-12-02.12.55,1960-12-02,84909dc1-9a60-44b3-a939-2393ab563089,ca.m.3212,Mr. Diefenbaker:,Prime Minister,PROVISION FOR CONTINUANCE OF RAILWAY OPERATIONS,,,I have not belonged to that group. In 1950 I took a strong and firm stand-and have throughout the years- against that form of legislation.

It has been said by the hon. member for Vancouver East that there should be a continuation of the conciliation processes provided for in the legislation. At any time an agreement is arrived at, this legislation ceases to be effective. I want to see these people together. We brought them together; we endeavoured to ascertain whether there was any possibility of agreement. I have said, and I repeat, that there was not that attitude on the part of either that would bring about anything in the nature of an agreement, reasonable in its characteristics. The preamble of the bill reads:

Whereas the processes of collective bargaining between the major railway companies and the representatives of their non-operating employees have failed to produce agreement, and the public interest requires that further efforts to react
agreement be resumed at a more favourable time without prejudice to the rights of either party and without interruption of the railway service;
Further on, in paragraph 3, we find the following:

Subject to this act, the term of each existing collective agreement is extended to include the period beginning on the commencement of this act and ending on the day on which a new collective agreement between the parties thereto in amendment or revision thereof comes into effect.

This makes every provision for a continuation of the conciliation proceedings. More than that, I think these people should be brought together at once. We continue the railways in operation. I for one will do everything I can to bring them together and regularly call them together so as to assure that discussions will continue and that justice will be done. So far as unfairness to the employees is concerned, there can be no justification for any truculent attitude being taken toward them.

There is one thing that I must answer, namely the suggestion that we in any way had acted for the benefit of the C.P.R. On the one hand, it was said and repeated that the Canadian Pacific railway wanted a strike to put the men in their places. That has been repeated here on more than one occasion. It must have been asserted with knowledge or it would not have been asserted, although I have no knowledge of that fact. If that is so, this legislation is a most effective answer to those who say there was any relationship between the Canadian Pacific and the government in this regard, because the tragic results which would follow such an attitude shall not and will not be countenanced.

I want to underline and emphasize that once again. The suggestion that that railway company would endeavour to do this to the workers of this country is such an outrageous one that if it has any foundation in fact, we have met it by preserving completely and absolutely the rights of labour and assuring at the same time the operation of the railways.

As far as the Canadian National Railways management are concerned, while the government has no authority over them-it is a separate and independent organization, and any interference in any way would be immediately challenged as improper and unjustifiable-I want to make it perfectly clear that if the management of the railway does things that ought not to be tolerated, that will do injustice to the workers of this country, this government, while scrupulously maintaining independence of that railway, will

Maintenance of Railway Operation Act certainly have the attention of the management brought to any such unfairness or discrimination against any of the workers of that railway. I want that definitely understood.

It has been a trying problem, sir, for all of us. We have tried to discharge our responsibilities. We have recognized that there will be misinterpretation of what we have done; that there will be endeavours to take political advantage of the course of action, as though we were in fact freezing wages to the detriment of the worker. As I said, we will maintain the conciliation processes from now until May 15. Instead of fixing a date away beyond, we fixed it in May so there would be no unjustified prolongation of the problem. We will bring these people together from time to time. Then, as I pointed out before, as soon as the freight rate freeze is lifted we will be in a position to bring about measures such as the hon. member for Assiniboia said were necessary to remove injustices and discriminatory rates, as far as that can be achieved, and the railways will be in a position to proceed in the only way in which expenses can be paid, namely either by grants or subsidies from parliament, in which case it comes out of the people through taxation, or through freight rates, which means that the users must pay additional amounts because of the increased expenses of operation.

We say this, and I repeat; it has been a difficult problem. I think parliament in the action it will take or is taking, provided that this bill is passed, to bring about a period not of inaction but of continued discussion between the parties, is doing the right thing. I believe the voice of reason will be heard; that public opinion has a tremendous influence on the production, the generation and the maintenance of reasonable, good common sense. If not, when we lift the freeze we will give the assurance that those who are workers on the railways, with their unions representing them, will be able to present their case, and that whatever is substituted in the place of the present agreements will be retroactive in fact to January 1, 1960.

There is no prejudice; there is postponement in order to prevent a strike taking place. Instead of taking the other course and bringing in compulsory arbitration, as suggested by the opposition-that in effect is what they say-we took the course we believed to be reasonable, namely the maintenance inviolate of the rights of labour, at the same time maintaining the public interest and welfare of 17,500,000 other Canadians. I think that in the process of time, as this becomes apparent and the rights of both sides become clear in the perspective of the days
Maintenance of Railway Operation Act ahead, what we have done will turn out to have been the proper and, indeed, the only course, the course of reason and of common sense.

My remarks will be brief and I hope, unemotional. However, at this point I would like to state the differences which exist between this group and the other parties in this house.

We believe, as do the other parties, that there should be no railway strike. We do not believe there should be any compulsion on workers to work at a wage level which has been found unacceptable by all standards and which would be unacceptable to any fair-minded Canadian. We do not believe that workers should be prepared to compromise themselves and compromise their fellow workers by doing so.

On the other hand, we do not believe that we in this house should legislate to the effect that management should pay, either. I think the Minister of Labour and the Prime Minister made a very good point when they suggested that there might be a time in the future when the house would be faced with similar legislation when the unions will have refused to accept a majority report of a conciliation board. On the other hand, I also accept the statement of the Leader of the Opposition
that he does not wish for an arbitrary solution. He believes there should be free play as between workers and management.

However, we believe that when parliament has to legislate in a situation such as this, neither labour nor management should be put at a disadvantage. That is why this group believe that if there is a national emergency the people of this nation would be willing to allow a favourable atmosphere to occur, an atmosphere in which neither management nor labour would be at a disadvantage. Here again, I think the former minister of transport had a good point when he called attention to the fact that this was an unusual situation because freight rates are frozen. By May 15 freight rates will be unfrozen and the royal commission report will have come down. At that time I am sure there will be a favourable atmosphere, because the workers will not be at a disadvantage and neither will management because they are not being obliged, through legislation, to pay higher wages.

I think this is the basis upon which a statesmanlike decision can be achieved. I think this is the basis upon which the citizens of Canada would be prepared to accept a subsidy until May 15 which, as the Prime Minister has pointed out, would amount to very little. On this basis I believe a change of atmosphere could occur immediately, a change which would bring together labour and management, and allow them to continue negotiations and, perhaps more than anything else, find a standard which would be acceptable and reasonable for the nonoperative railway workers, one which would be much higher than that suggested in the majority report of the conciliation board.

2080265,ca.proc.d.1960-12-02.12.104,1960-12-02,0daa460f-b2c1-447e-abbe-c4bd1f237b32,ca.m.6630,Mr. Hazen Argue (Assiniboia):,,PROVISION FOR CONTINUANCE OF RAILWAY OPERATIONS,,,Mr. Speaker, before we take this vote, I should like very briefly to go over the main points of criticism and the main propositions that are being put forward by our group at this time.

Our first position is that this legislation should not have been necessary; that the government might have taken another course that would have solved the problem, and would not have placed parliament in the position of having to deal with legislation that we think is repugnant to the Canadian way of life, is undemocratic and should not be embarked upon by any free parliament except in a very extreme emergent situation, which we think did not need to arise.

We agree with all those who have said that everything possible should be done to avoid a strike; that a strike would bring difficulty perhaps chaos to many communities and industries in this country, and that management, workers and government should together have been able to bring forward a proposition that would have avoided a strike.

Beyond question there is compulsion in this bill. This is what the bill is about; it is to force the railway workers and the companies to maintain and continue operations until May 15. The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) said that this is not compulsory arbitration. He argues that after May 15 next year the parties will go back to their original position. In this legislation he has failed to give anything to the workers involved. The attitude of the Liberal party is that had there been in this legislation a provision for
compulsory arbitration along the lines of the legislation of 1950, they would have been in support of it.

2080268,ca.proc.d.1960-12-02.12.107,1960-12-02,0daa460f-b2c1-447e-abbe-c4bd1f237b32,ca.m.6630,Mr. Argue:,,PROVISION FOR CONTINUANCE OF RAILWAY OPERATIONS,,,The position of the Liberal party is that this kind of legislation with that provision added is something that they could support. We are opposed to this legislation, as we were opposed to the legislation in 1950. We are opposed to compulsion without arbitration; we are opposed to compulsion with arbitration. We feel that the workers have a good case. The Prime Minister has admitted it, the Liberal party in the house has stated it and we have stated it, and yet in this legislation nothing is being done to recognize that principle; and so the workers involved are exceedingly disappointed with what is now taking place.

I have said on a previous occasion that in our judgment the C.P.R. was in a financial position to meet the majority report of the conciliation board. However, it is understandable that the Canadian Pacific railway would dig in its heels and say no when they became aware that the government would bring about this kind of legislation which would remove the pressure that the workers had been able to place on the railways. The government assured the railway and the country that the company would continue operations even without an increase in wages, and therefore the company had nothing to lose.

We have suggested that, as an alternative to the compulsion in the bill presented by the government, as an alternative to the compulsion that the Liberal party is prepared to support, there is and there was another way out, where compulsion would not have been necessary, where the government might have taken action to resolve the problem in a way that would help the workers and the Canadian public. We suggested that a subsidy should be paid from the national treasury and that this subsidy at least from now on until May 15, and perhaps beyond that, would have removed the grievance of the workers and the opposition of the railway companies to signing an agreement. We think this was a reasonable proposition. The government will argue and does argue that a subsidy in this instance is wrong. The Liberal party is not prepared to support this kind of a subsidy. We suggest that a subsidy of this size for this purpose at this time is a much fairer way to deal with this question than the attitude taken by the government to force the men back to work and say that next May 15 our policy is to load the additional wages on to the freight users of this country.

What the Prime Minister has said is that a strike next spring may be possible. He said that the government is removing the right to strike at this time, not the right to strike in the future. The Prime Minister is saying that with the restoration of the rights of free men in this situation an application can then be made to the board of transport commissioners. As I see it, what will happen, what the government intends to happen, is a very large increase in freight rates next spring. It wants to bring about the postponement of the problem until then at which time the burden of the increase will be loaded on the freight service users of the country.

As a matter of fact, an additional part of their policy has become clear, namely that the subsidy now in effect for the purpose of maintaining freight rates as they exist will be withdrawn and the country will face a very large and, I am positive, discriminatory increase in freight rates because it is practically impossible to bring about a complete equality of all freight rates even though, as I have said, I have great confidence in M. A. MacPherson, the chairman of the royal commission.
We do not reject subsidies as part of a national policy. We think it is time for a general transportation policy that will provide parity of treatment to the workers.

Pickersgill (Bonavisla-Twillin-gate):,,PROVISION FOR CONTINUANCE OF RAILWAY OPERATIONS,,,Mr. Speaker, before the vote is taken I should like to correct a misstatement that the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) made-I do not accuse him of being intentional about this-with respect to the position of the Liberal party. As I heard him say it, he said that this legislation would be acceptable to the Liberal party if it provided for compulsory arbitration. That, of course, is completely wrong.

What the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) said this morning was that this legislation would be acceptable to the Liberal party if it was amended to impose the terms recommended in the majority report of the conciliation board. That is not arbitration but rather a determination by parliament which is a very different thing. We are concerned with an agreement that expired on December 31, 1959 and is only continued in operation by the general law, and under the bill we are determining that that shall be the agreement. We think that if we are going to impose settlement by parliament, and that is what the government is asking us to do, the settlement imposed by parliament should be one that was determined independently to be fair. That is our position.

The government is asking parliament to compel the men to stay at work, and we support that, but the government is also compelling the men to stay at work at wages that the men refuse to regard as fair and reasonable, and we do not support that. We think, as the Leader of the Opposition said, that if you are going to compel the men to stay at work the companies should be compelled to pay between now and next May the amounts determined in the majority award, that there should be no subsidy now but that next May or June or whenever it is-here we differ completely with the C.C.F.-a general review

Maintenance of Railway Operation Act be made after the report of the royal commission, which we do not think should be prejudged and any disability to the railways resulting from this imposition should then be taken into account in the policy determined by parliament. That is the position we take.

We are not suggesting that in this case there should be compulsory arbitration. There is nothing to arbitrate. There are two positions. The companies say that they do not want to pay anything more. The men say that they are satisfied with the majority award. When I said there was nothing to arbitrate I was perhaps wrong. An arbitration would involve the determination of something in between these two positions. That is what an arbitration would do. We are not in favour of arbitration. If parliament is going to compel the men to work, we are in favour of that compulsion being accompanied by compulsion on the companies to pay the wages that the independent chairman appointed by the government determined would be fair and reasonable in the circumstances.

BENIDICKSON    REFERENCE TO SPEECH OF MINISTER OF LABOUR,,,Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege which I think affects all hon. members of the house and which will certainly prove to affect the privileges of many outside the house.

Your Honour will appreciate our unusual difficulty today in that we sat until about two o'clock this morning and that was followed by an early morning sitting today. In consequence of this I was not able to look at my own Hansard until a few moments ago. I do not have the privileges of many others in the house who concurrent with the sittings of the house are supplied with blue sheets from Hansard.

I refer Your Honour to page 398 of Hansard of December 1 where the remarks of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) appear. I was aware at that time that I would likely shortly follow the minister who was concluding the debate on second reading and in consequence thereof I made very close notes of some of the pertinent remarks he was making. I made careful notes and I still have those notes in my hand. I find that in the first paragraph of his remarks yesterday he referred to ""the best possible way"" which I have here in quotation marks. In the second paragraph of his speech on page 398 in the left hand column I find to my surprise that he is reported to have said in that paragraph:
The purpose of this bill is to extend the present agreements to May 15 and to give the opportunity for collective bargaining-

At that point for the purposes of reply, as I indicated, I made notes. I distinctly heard the minister say that there would be given the opportunity after May 15 to strike. There is nothing in the text today that has reference to the words ""opportunity after May 15 to strike"". To establish that was elementary to my remarks during the course of the debate.

If Your Honour will look at the next page 400, in the right hand column, you will find that this subject also interested the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin). The hon. member for Essex East was questioning the minister as to the rights of the workers after May 15. In the right hand column on that page the hon. member for Essex East is reported as having said:
The government has said that all it is doing is postponing the situation. What will happen on May 15 if the men decide to strike?
I intervened at that point and said:
The minister has already said he will give them the opportunity to strike on May 15.
Questions of Privilege

I know that some ministers who, as I say, are supplied with blue sheets from Hansard and do not have to go to the debates office on the third floor as some of the rest of us do, occasionally have the assistance of their staff-their secretaries or executive assistants-in the revision of their Hansard text. I should like the minister to indicate to the house whether he personally made any elimination of the phrase I read from my notes or if not whether he would inquire and ascertain if any member of his staff made a correction in the Hansard text differing from the note I have outlined?

2080335,ca.proc.d.1960-12-02.18.1.1.1,1960-12-02,,,,stagedirection,,,,The house resumed, from Friday, November 25, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Starr-Mr. Flynn in the chair:

authority, including contributions toward the cost of capital expenditures on training facilities connected with such programs; to authorize the Minister of Labour to undertake programs of technical and vocational training for specified categories of persons; to provide for the establishment and operation of an advisory council and the appointment of its members and staff and to define its duties; and to provide for other related and incidental matters.

2080336,ca.proc.d.1960-12-02.18.1.2,1960-12-02,3c7abf33-5a24-4c46-87e9-5a6c9d457af5,ca.m.9967,Mr. Caron:,,VOCATIONAL TRAINING,PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL PROGRAMS,,"Mr. Chairman, a week ago I had to interrupt my remarks at the sounding of the six o'clock bell announcing the adjournment of the house. At that time I was saying that since the beginning of the session the government has suggested amendments to some acts that were already in our statutes, but without saying so forthright, leading us to believe that entirely new bills were being introduced.

As a matter of fact, in the resolution under consideration, there is only one thing different from the act of 1952 and the amendments of 1954, and that is the establishment of an advisory council, and nothing else. Now, we urge the government to consult with the provinces with a view to ensuring a more adequate training to those who are about to start on their own, and those who are already on the labour market and must change jobs when they are not completely ready to do so, especially day labourers. But the department should have entered into negotiations with the province before introducing this legislation. Because we know that education at all levels, comes under provincial jurisdiction. Now, suppose we pass the bill that will follow the resolution under discussion, what will happen if the provinces, not having been consulted, say no for some reason or other? We would have passed a totally ineffective bill.

With regard to the field of education, I wonder if French-Canadian members from the province of Quebec would like to make their opinion known to us, because we all know how they objected to the intervention of the federal government in this field. They have done so repeatedly since 1953, or since the Liberal government decided to assist universities. How can they agree to vote for such legislation today?

I probably could have asked the Secretary of State (Mr. Dorion) if he would care to make again the speeches he used to make before he accepted the joint responsibility of the cabinet, but I would not dare. I should like, however, that some Quebec member
Vocational Training

state his stand and that of his colleagues on this resolution. As for us, our mind is at rest. The Liberals have accepted and recognized that the federal government had the right to interfere in the field of education, in so far as the provinces agreed, and we shall pursue that course.

The present project is a long range one and we intend to endorse it. We recognize that its purpose is to prepare, in a rather distant future, the young generation so that it might play its part within society. But what is being done at the present time? Has the Department of Labour found a way to settle the present economic emergency, when thousands of workers seek employment and thousands of unemployed are unable to withdraw unemployment insurance benefits because they lack the required number of stamps?

Are we able to find, in this resolution, anything which might relieve the immediate plight? Even though I studied every resolution on the order paper, I found nothing which could remedy the present plight of our society.

We are all in favour of long term assistance projects, but we maintain that the government has the responsibility of trying to settle the immediate problem of those who are suffering from unemployment in spite of what the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) had promised, of those who do not have enough bread on their table or enough money to pay their rent and who have to ask the municipalities for help through direct relief.

At this time, the government is following the policy it has adopted in the past, which means that it is passing on its responsibility to the municipalities. Long term legislation can be proposed similar to that which we now have for consideration and which will take one, two or even three years to give results, but in the meantime the municipalities have to bear the heavy burden of unemployment, which is not due to the municipalities but to the carelessness of this administration which did not find the necessary markets for our production surpluses, with the result that we are overstocked with products of all kinds. Manufacturers are forced to idleness at least a few days a week, due to the fact that they cannot sell their surplus production.

That is what the federal government should have done, besides bringing down legislation such as the one now before us and which we support. But it should also have attended to the immediate situation. If it had followed our suggestions a year or two ago, when we warned the government that there was danger
Vocational Training

ahead and we submitted at least 25 suggestions for new legislation; if it had heeded the suggestions made by the opposition we would probably not be in such a predicament at this time. Unfortunately, the minister claimed at the time that the problem was just temporary. He was listening to advice from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) who was satisfied that the recession was over and that we were on our way to prosperity.

Well, Mr. Chairman, we find today that the advice of the Minister of Finance was based on nothing but his own intuition and that we are now faced with a much more serious situation. If the government has decided to offer effective legislation, I submit that that legislation should be amended in order to be of greater assistance to the younger generation.
I would also ask the government to try and find means to help the needy at this time.

It should not be forgotten, Mr. Chairman, that communism does not thrive on people's prosperity, but on their distress. If these hard times were to continue, people of good will will be seen throwing overboard old principles that they used to hold dear and give themselves to the highest bidder.
The government has some responsibilities, and it should find the ways and means to relieve the present want while getting ready to give assistance to those who tomorrow will have to change jobs.

In view of these facts and the present needs and in the light of this bill, I would ask all members, and especially the Conservative members, to abstain from anything that might delay their own bill so that it can be put into force as soon as possible in order that we may bring forward as soon as possible, bills meant to cope immediately with this unemployment situation which is affecting our population. Thus shall we contribute to the greatest happiness of all, and the Liberal party will readily support this resolution.

,Liberal,,Alexis Pierre Caron,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=3c7abf33-5a24-4c46-87e9-5a6c9d457af5&Language=E&Section=ALL
2080337,ca.proc.d.1960-12-02.18.1.3,1960-12-02,9b3d80e9-bd09-42be-a80f-3ac040e3c940,ca.m.8466,Mr. Best:,,VOCATIONAL TRAINING,PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL PROGRAMS,,Mr. Chairman, I am delighted to rise in support of this most important long range measure. I have listened with interest, as I am sure others have, to the hon. member for Hull. We have no difficulty whatsoever, of course, in hearing him. His voice carries very well. However, I did have difficulty in understanding just what he said and what relation it had to the present measure. He discussed many other subjects.

I feel that the measure now before us could have tremendously beneficial effects on unemployment, on industrial manpower and on productivity in Canada in the near future and, indeed, over the long range years ahead. I can think of few measures more vital and more contributory to advancement within our country. There are a number of important problems facing us today and with the changes in technology in our present world and the ever-narrowing horizons of our world today, trained manpower and skilled people are of paramount importance to our country.

When one studies the figures one notices that in the ranks of the unemployed today there are people who in many instances are not specifically trained in a particular skill so as to be able to fill certain positions. In his speech, as found in Hansard of November 25, pages 231 and 232, the Minister of Labour remarked in the ranks of the unemployed the unskilled are approximately three times as numerous as unemployed workers who have specific training or skills. I think this is indicative of the problem before us and the government is taking steps to bring about increased assistance in this regard.

We realize that education in general comes within the sphere of provincial action but in collaboration with the provinces I am sure that the government can advance at present and even more so in the future, the important cause of technical education in our country. Many people have come to Canada in the last 15 years, as a matter of fact somewhere in the neighbourhood of two million, I believe, and we have tried in most instances to bring to Canada those with specific skills who could contribute something to agricultural and industrial production and other important projects within our country. We sometimes see, and this is the unhappy thing, that it is our native born Canadians who are unemployed and who, because of lack of specific training and knowlege to enable them to be fitted into our increasingly complex industrial situation, sometimes cannot avail themselves of the jobs that are open and waiting.

The minister pointed out in his speech, to which I referred earlier, that while there may be numbers of unemployed there are jobs without job-takers in various areas because of a lack of people in the particular area who are specifically trained. I think one of our problems in this regard is perhaps a psychological one that our country will have to face in the present circumstances and in future years. I refer to the recognition of the

dignity and importance of technical training for our people. We are conscious of the tremendous increase in high school and university education and in the need for plant and other facilities, and more teachers and professors, but we must also realize that with the increasing raising of standards in university education and the increasing volume of enrolment not all of our children can make the best and wisest use of that sort of training. In other words, technical training at some level of secondary education in the high schools and, indeed, at the age level of university education, may be a much wiser course for many young people who are coming of age, as it were, to follow.

The minister has pointed out the interesting fact that in the next five years, I presume up to 1965, more than half a million young Canadians will enter the labour market. This very large number of young people coming forward for education and training must in my opinion have in front of them an increased scope for learning and acquiring the skills which are so highly necessary in this day and age. It is because of this that I feel that a long range attack on the sort of technological unemployment that we see in Canada today must be made through constructive measures of this sort.

In a field such as the construction industry and in home building which our government has aided so much in the last three years, we know that as the rise and fall of home building-the flow as it were in this industry -goes, so does a considerable amount of employment or unemployment in various areas. That result is natural. But sometimes these people are unable through lack of skills, when home building has caught up in certain areas, as it has to some extent at least, to fit into other jobs through lack of specific technical training.

I should like to comment on some other remarks made by the minister in this direction. He mentioned the fact that there are large numbers of men and women unemployed for lack of essential skills. He has mentioned and I have quoted the fact that as to the untrained jobless, as it were, the ranks of the unemployed are swelled by these people to a much larger extent. I think we should be truly troubled by these figures. I thought it of great interest to note on page 233 of Hansard the minister's figures indicating that some 5 per cent of all young people enrolled in our secondary schools are taking a technical course program and that of post-high school technical students in Canada-as I presume this figure means- some 8,000 are enrolled in straight technical schools or programs apart from our high
Vocational Training

schools. These figures are really low. They are fantastically low in a country like Canada, a country such as we have here with a small ribbon-like population stretched over a great area, and which must depend now and in the future on our competitive ability to do things better and in a more productive fashion in order to compete with other markets and with other countries around the world which have a longer tradition in technical training and a much larger labour pool.

This measure, of course, ties in as well with the most interesting mention and presentation of a productivity council for Canada, for technical training is closely allied to increased productivity and greater efficiency of industry, agriculture and production of all sorts within our country. I am sure this productivity council will want to work closely in the future with any system or systems of technical education on a municipal, provincial or federal level. These are some of the things which we are examining today.

We have brought to Canada people from many other lands. The minister has pointed out in the past that these countries, of course, have certain differences in programs. They are older countries with longer traditions and perhaps smaller areas and a growth that has been more stable over a longer period of years but not so dynamic as is ours. These countries have the institutions and the facilities with which to train their young people and indeed to train their unemployed for the minister has mentioned that as well as the young people themselves, we must put into effect some scheme or some program by means of which to train and, as it were, almost to rehabilitate for increased usefulness in society some of those who at the present time do not have jobs and positions. The over-all effect of this program I am certain will be of the utmost importance in the years ahead.

As Canada grows and as our population enlarges and as the course of technical progress increases, not decreases-for I am sure it is increasing-this problem of unemployment, this problem of workers fitting into specific positions will enlarge. Our young people and our people of all ages must, if possible, have more basic technical training in order to enable them to have a flexibility to shift from one job to another. On the job training, while useful and while most important, in many instances must be backed by a basic training in a variety of technical fields that can be applied to a variety and wide spectrum of jobs. As technical progress continues I am sure that the sort of move proposed here today will be of most fundamental importance in solving our unemployment problem in Canada and indeed in the
Vocational Training
positive sense aiding in increasing the productivity, the usefulness and the happiness throughout the whole of our land.

,Progressive Conservative,,Charles Alexander (Sandy) Best,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=9b3d80e9-bd09-42be-a80f-3ac040e3c940&Language=E&Section=ALL
2080338,ca.proc.d.1960-12-02.18.1.4,1960-12-02,b815a117-7953-4900-b152-afc56dfc44a1,ca.m.5560,Mr. Herridge:,,VOCATIONAL TRAINING,PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL PROGRAMS,,Mr. Chairman, I rise on behalf of this group to express our support for the purpose and principle of this resolution. However, in doing that, may I say that we are looking forward to seeing the details of the bill in order to make certain that the legislation is comprehensive enough to meet a great and growing need with respect to the technical education of our young people in this country.

I want to place before the committee a few of my opinions with respect to this resolution. I would not for a moment attempt to compete with the dynamic, expansive, impulsive and propulsive hon. member for Hull. However, I am going to utilize my meagre talents in this field in order to give the committee my opinion with respect to this measure.

It is an important measure having regard to the fact that what we do in this field will have a great effect upon the future of hundreds of thousands of young Canadians. There are great possibilities for the development of human character and human happiness and for the promotion of human usefulness in the proper application of the legislation suggested by this resolution. As mentioned by the hon. member who spoke previously, there is a phenomenon that is being noticed more and more across the country, namely the growing percentage of unskilled workers in Canada who are unable to obtain employment. I notice it in my own district, and I am sure it is very general indeed. Also being noticed is the increasing number of boys and girls leaving school who do not go beyond grade eight. When that happens I say there is something wrong with our school curriculums when children are not attracted and inspired in the first instance to continue on with their senior education. Then in other instances there is not the native ability or the desire to follow an academic form of education.

When I say that, may I say that I have had some experience with schools, having been chairman of a school board for a good many years and having had to work with teachers on problems related to the administration of schools. It is a fact that increasing numbers of young people are leaving school on arriving at grade eight or less and are not going on to senior education. If we make ample allowance for those who are not naturally inclined or have not the capacity to go on with academic education, there is something wrong when that situation continues to get worse and worse. We have the largest investment, the best equipment and the best

brained teachers we have ever had in Canadian history so far as schools are concerned, on the lower level particularly, as compared to the little red school houses of from 25 years to 50 years ago-well do I remember them- when children walked three miles to school through three feet of snow and were happy to do so. Now they must be taken there in a bus, and we build a gymnasium in the school in order to give them some exercise so their physical condition will be maintained.

However, I mention this because I am very interested in this question. I see so much of the need for training in my own district. I know of young people whose lives are actually being wasted because they lack the training and the opportunity to attain the skills that are necessary in our technological society.

We need electricians; we need men in the construction industry; we need plumbers; we need bricklayers. It would surprise one to find how difficult it is to obtain first-class tradesmen in the rural areas of Canada. It is difficult to obtain a first-class bricklayer, for example, to build1 a chimney or a wall, or things of that sort. It is also difficult to get plumbers in the smaller communities, because tradesmen are not inclined to go to these smaller communities to obtain a living.

There are some opportunities for tradesmen who want to build up small businesses in many of the smaller communities of this country. I say this from my own experience in the southeastern portion of British Columbia. Also, there is a great opportunity for the training of technicians in the forest industry, in highway construction and other types of construction projects being undertaken throughout this country.

In my opinion we are wasting human resources in two ways. First of all we are wasting human resources because they are untrained technically or as tradesmen to do the things that require to be done to satisfactorily perform the services required in connection with the types of employment I have mentioned. Second, we are wasting human resources in this way. I have had some experience with construction; I have had charge of building a good many miles of highways, and bridges through mountains and in rocky country, through a great deal of rock where thousands of yards of rock or earth had to be moved, and with very primitive equipment compared to nowadays. We are wasting human resources in this respect, because I repeatedly see engineers being^ used to perform a job that a good technician or tradesman could properly perform.

2080342,ca.proc.d.1960-12-02.19.3,1960-12-02,b815a117-7953-4900-b152-afc56dfc44a1,ca.m.5560,Mr. Herridge:,,I960,,,No; I must say it is a very hard thing to explain. I am not saying there is a surplus of trained engineers and personnel; I am saying that I have known a great many instances where a man with engineering degrees has had to go some hundreds of miles to perform work such as I have mentioned in connection with these types of projects; that is, to perform some rather elementary service in connection with these projects, when a well-trained technician or tradesman could have performed the service.

There were plenty of men on the job who could run bulldozers or earth-moving equipment, who could push wheel barrows and handle picks, shovels, air-drills and that sort of thing, but there was not, in a gang of 100 or more workmen, a man who could take an ordinary level and transmit his readings to paper and lay out, say, a simple cut and fill program along an easy grade.

I mention that because I think there has been a waste of human resources in the unnecessary use of highly trained people, particular in the industries I have mentioned. That is why I think there is a tremendous opportunity for comprehensive legislation that meets the need in this connection and does something to fill this gap between the unskilled and university trained.

The minister was quite correct when he said that European countries have long recognized the formal paths necessary to acquire occupational skills. That is known from European history and the history of the development of technical and trade schools in Great Britain. We have been very laggard in this respect, as indicated by the number
Vocational Training

of persons attending technical schools at the present time. If I heard the minister correctly, the figure is 8,000 students attending technical schools at the present time in a country like this where we have a need for hundreds of thousands of technically trained men and tradesmen.

There is a very narrow margin, shall I say, between a technician and a first-class tradesman in many instances. I was also glad to hear that the government intends to continue research into this problem, because it is a serious question.

There are others who are spending some time studying this question. I was very glad to hear recently that the Canadian welfare council, just from the point of view of the welfare of human beings, is undertaking a very careful study of our manpower needs and the need for technical training, and intends to make representations to the committee of the other place. Also I saw in a press dispatch of November 30 that an interesting representation was made to the committee of the other place by the columnist Mr. F. T. Denton of Toronto. This was an analysis of employment and unemployment in Canada during the past ten years. He said in that report:

Young persons, the unskilled and the less educated are providing Canada with its hard core of unemployment. And if the current trend continues, one million new jobs will be needed in the next five years to absorb the flow of new workers and cut existing unemployment levels to half.
These are pretty startling figures when we are dealing with a problem like this, and I am very pleased to see that there is a growing interest and concern with this question.

The minister mentioned that this system of technical and trade schools was much more advanced in European countries, which is quite correct. I sent to the library for a few books and pamphlets on this question, and I have here a pamphlet issued by the central office of information, reference division, entitled Technological Education in Britain. It is rather interesting. It indicates the possibilities for us. We are only starting in this field in Canada.

I note here that technical education and training first commenced in Great Britain about 1824, as a result of a similar situation to that which is happening in Canada at the present time, but on a much minor scale there. The system progressed very slowly indeed; the tempo of technical education did not really accelerate until the latter part of the Victorian era.
However, to indicate the opportunities which are set out in this pamphlet, there is
Vocational Training

the national college of horology and instrument technology, the national foundry college-a college for foundry workers-the national college for heating, ventilating, refrigeration and fan engineering, the national college of rubber technology, the national leathersellers' college, the national college of food technology, the Scottish woollen technical college, and many others. I just mention those to illustrate the possibilities there are for the development of technical schools to provide training in the skills so badly needed in this country.

I am interested in this problem because first of all it is a Canadian problem. It is a widespread and urgent Canadian problem. I am also very interested in the problem because it is of serious concern to my constituents. Because it is a growing problem, school boards in our province have been urging the provincial government to take advantage of the grants that can be obtained from the federal government under the present vocational training act.

We have had vocational training in schools for years. In my opinion, while it is very satisfactory for, shall I say, the elementary teaching of certain trades and abilities and the acquisition of manual skills, and so on, you cannot train technical personnel and tradesmen along with high school students. Success will require a separate school system entirely where young people who have left high school can enter to be trained as technicians or tradesmen.

That is where the whole scheme has to be well planned by the provinces. I understand that under this legislation the initiative will have to come from the provinces. I hope they respond to this legislation and that it will not be a hit-or-miss affair on their part. Surely, our government in British Columbia, with its knowledge of the population and industrial development in the province together with its projection as to the development which can be expected for some years in the future, can plan a system of technical and trade schools to meet the needs of the young people who require training. I trust it will exercise its initiative and co-operate with the federal government in making the legislation envisaged by this resolution a success. This is important to my constituents.

In many cases people who are desirous of attending training schools or technical schools have been denied that opportunity because of the distances which they would have to travel or, often, because of the cost. These schools will have to be fairly close to the persons they are intended to serve and I suggest that in addition to schools to serve
[Mr. Herridge.l
Vancouver island and the main coastal area we shall need establishments to serve southeastern and central British Columbia.
