2080343,ca.proc.d.1960-12-02.19.4,1960-12-02,82878bc6-6bd2-407b-b2cc-7745aec02c2a,ca.m.8707,Mr. Macdonnell:,,I960,,,Did the hon. gentleman mean, when he spoke earlier of technical training as distinct from university training, that the technical training must be clearly and absolutely technical, that the students must devote all their time to technical instruction?

,Progressive Conservative,,James MacKerras Macdonnell,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=82878bc6-6bd2-407b-b2cc-7745aec02c2a&Language=E&Section=ALL
2080344,ca.proc.d.1960-12-02.19.5,1960-12-02,b815a117-7953-4900-b152-afc56dfc44a1,ca.m.5560,Mr. Herridge:,,I960,,,The hon. gentleman must realize that I am a simple backwoodsman with no pretence to higher educational achievement. I speak from experience rather than as one who has had a great deal of academic education or who holds academic degrees. However, I think there is a time when students have to decide whether they are going on to higher academic achievement or whether to leave high school and confine their activities to technical or trade school training. My point was that I do not think it is possible to combine satisfactorily trade training and technical training with the rest of the curriculum inside high schools. While I am interested in teachers in high school teaching vocational training, manual skills, to the higher grade pupils, that is a separate function.

Now I have given a complete outline of my ideas in this respect. All hon. members may not agree with me, but I speak from some experience and knowledge of the problem. Let me say again, in conclusion, that I trust the present legislation is comprehensive enough to meet an increasing need and I sincerely hope the provinces concerned will respond to this opportunity.

,Co-operative Commonwealth Federation (C.C.F.),,Herbert Wilfred Herridge,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=b815a117-7953-4900-b152-afc56dfc44a1&Language=E&Section=ALL
2080345,ca.proc.d.1960-12-02.19.6,1960-12-02,00163189-b2e2-4300-9100-81f7d68a7930,ca.m.4256,Mr. Horner (Acadia):,,I960,,,I think this is a well worth-while measure. Any measure which encourages technical and vocational training is certainly worth supporting, and this ties in nicely with all the other good measures referred to in the speech from the throne. I, too, would like to see this bill brought in as soon as possible, but before that time I should like to suggest a few thoughts which I hope may be reflected in the measure when it is enacted.

With automation advancing at a very fast pace in this highly mechanized North American continent, I think there is a great need for increased technical and vocational training. I am in agreement with the hon. member for Kootenay West that technical and vocational training should be on a higher level than the standard at which it is taught in high schools. I think a person graduating from a vocational or technical school should be able to come out with a degree which will qualify him as a person who has real ability in the field he has chosen to take up.

The province of Alberta from which I come is fast developing into a manufacturing province. Its population is growing rapidly and it is now, I think, the fourth largest province in Canada as far as population is concerned. Because of the success of the oil and gas industry in that province, manufacturing has come to play a prominent part in its development.

Along with the hon. member for Kootenay West, I believe there is a growing need for trained workers. A figure which is not often talked about shows that three out of four jobs becoming available today require a person with a higher education or skill in some trade. This is particularly evident in the province of Alberta as well as in Canada in general. In some of the older countries, particularly in Europe, greater stress is perhaps placed upon sending a person out into the world with a skill or trade of some kind at his disposal. For centuries people grew up in the older countries of the world and, instead of just continuing in school, branched out in the field or skill in which they were trained so as to better equip themselves to compete. Certainly, there are any number of trades which a person can take up-plumbing, electric wiring or electronics, for example. Then, under vocational training, there is a need for butchers and other such trades.

I was interested to hear the hon. member for Kootenay West say there was a great need in some of the rural areas for plumbers and electricians. Men could easily earn a living by going out into some of these rural areas and, possibly, many will be ready to do so after the schools have been set up. I know that in my own constituency, which is largely a rural constituency, there is always a need for plumbers or electricians, whose skills seem to be in high demand. Even in the field of agriculture, with which I am closely connected, there is a growing need for persons with some degree of skill and, in some instances, a high degree of skill. Many advances have been made in the past few years and now we find a large number of farms highly dieselized and highly mechanized, so much so that a farmer has to be a jack of all trades and know a lot about a great number of things if he is to succeed.

In Alberta we have several schools of agriculture, and I graduated from one of them, but I have always thought they could go on and teach highly technical skills in those schools rather than deal in the generalities which some of the subjects cover. They should perhaps give greater training in motor mechanics. Dieselization on the farms has increased the need for this training. Hydraulics today play an important part on the farm. Many farmers find that they require
Vocational Training
some knowledge of the subject in order to fit their equipment with hydraulic appliances and measures that will make farming easier and more economical for them.

Together with more stress on motor mechanics greater emphasis should be placed on meat preparation, butchering and other courses relating to animal husbandry. I was pleased to note that the veterinary college in Ontario has an extensive course relating to various types of meat. Certainly this training would better equip a person who was going into butchering or even someone who planned to engage in raising livestock. This too has become highly competitive and highly technical with the implementation of hormones into the feeding rations of livestock. If more extensive teaching were done in relation to these subjects students leaving agricultural colleges or vocational schools would be better equipped to get along in their respective fields.

With the introduction of these grants some hon. members feared that the federal government was invading the domain of provinces in the field of education. I am sure that most hon. gentlemen realize that the grants will be made available on a shared basis with the provinces by request. As an hon. member from Alberta I hope that my home province will be able to take advantage of these grants thereby better preparing the young people to compete and enjoy life in the years ahead.

,Progressive Conservative,,John (Jack) Henry Horner,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=00163189-b2e2-4300-9100-81f7d68a7930&Language=E&Section=ALL
2080346,ca.proc.d.1960-12-02.19.7,1960-12-02,57dd42c2-427c-4252-9a45-f0c416cc0e1b,ca.m.5944,Mr. Pitman:,,I960,,,Mr. Chairman, as a new member I hesitate to inflict myself on the committee twice in one day but I did want to congratulate the Minister of Labour on bringing this resolution before the committee and to express my earnest hope that it will be introduced as legislation in the very near future.

I rise on this question because I am particularly interested in the area of education. Until only four or five weeks ago I was taking part in education on a full-time scale in another place. Possibly some hon. members would prefer it if I were still doing so.

If this measure is to come up to the expectations of the people of Canada and merit the congratulations of those who sit in this corner of the chamber I think it must fulfil four very important requirements. It must be a dynamic and all-inclusive attempt to meet the needs of every community in these two areas, the training of the unemployed and the training of our young people to meet the demands of this new technological age.
Vocational Training

Second, this proposed legislation surely must be completely adaptable to every community in this nation so that every community will be able to apply to a provincial legislature and take advantage of this measure.
Third, I hope this will be a first step toward a whole new concept of the responsibility of the federal government in the education and training of our youth.
Finally, I hope this will be a part of a new approach to our whole economy for if this proposed legislation is to be effective it must relate itself to a planned, integrated economy.

Unfortunately in the past the whole program of training the unemployed has been most inadequate. Reference has already been made to the Vocational Training Co-Ordination Act passed in 1952 and amended in 1954. As originally envisaged the act was to enable the minister to undertake projects to provide vocational training to fit unemployed persons for gainful employment. In 1954 it was amended to include a provision designed to fit persons for employment for any purpose in the national interest within the legislative authority of the parliament of Canada and approved by the governor in council.

I am not blaming the federal government for the inadequate situation that has obtained in this respect. As I understand it, in many cases the provinces did not even take advantage of the grants that were available. However, across Canada between April, 1958 and March, 1959 there were only 3,568 people trained. I think there were more unemployed in my own constituency last winter than were trained under this program in the whole of Canada. Federal assistance applied for by the provinces in this respect amounted to only $510,479.99.

In a country in which unemployment is a very serious problem surely that is not the scale on which this problem must be met. In Ontario, between April, 1958 and March 31, 1959 there were 94 men and 32 women who were re-trained. I suggest that this problem will not be solved on that scale. The report of the director of Canadian vocational training indicated that the number asking for assistance was not as large as expected. And yet what was the need?

A pamphlet put out by the Department of Labour on the training of skilled manpower admitted that training facilities in Canada were failing to keep pace with the requirement for manpower and that we were importing skilled labour from the United Kingdom and Europe. A winter research program was undertaken to discover the level of ability and training in several areas. It was found, for example, in relation to tool and

diemakers that only 8.5 per cent of Canadian tradesmen in this field had received secondary education in appropriate technical training whereas 46 per cent of non-Canadian tool and diemakers had received adequate training in this trade. That is a commentary upon vocational training throughout this nation as it takes place in the provinces.

If this program is to have a sufficient impact to be of any use in the twentieth century it must be undertaken on a scale that will make everything we have done before look absolutely ridiculous. It is significant that in my own riding of Peterborough we have a general union of unemployed workers. I hope this union will not grow very much stronger but if the situation worsens it may well become the largest union in the riding.

These men have done more than whine about their situation. They are in a serious plight. While perhaps they are not dropping in the streets they are nevertheless suffering mentally and spiritually. Rather than whine about their plight they have taken positive steps through every level of government to provide this kind of training for their members through the hard winter. It is only through re-training that the unemployed will solve their problems when they feel that once again they can make a useful contribution to the community where they live. It is not a matter of accepting a dole. They do not want unemployment insurance. What they want is to return, so to speak, to Canadian society in a useful, vital capacity. I hope this resolution will help these people.

It is important that this program be adaptable to each community. Technical institutions cannot be built in some communities which are too small to support them. I hope this resolution will provide grants whereby these areas may perhaps use the money to provide for their unemployed transportation to some other centre where there is a technical institution that can provide the type of training these people need. I hope it will provide grants not just for buildings but for areas which have buildings which may be used. I suggest vocational schools which might be used from four o'clock in the afternoon until seven or eight o'clock at night. I hope it may possibly provide money for teaching and also for the maintenance of equipment in a great many areas where people could be trained adequately and on the basis of what is possible in the community in which those unemployed people live. It is possible that there will be need to provide assistance to men so that they can take those courses and not mean a hardship to their wives and families when they are actually taking part
in the course. I hope that the legislation will be not only dynamic and all-inclusive, but that it will also be adaptable.

I hope it will provide a new motivation for vocational training. I think that unfortunately we in Canada have never come to acquire the kind of feeling which people in European countries and the United Kingdom have for their crafts. I think we need to motivate people in the direction of vocational training, and instil in them a pride in vocational training. Too often vocational training has become a kind of second rate education. It has been suggested that a vocational school is a dumping ground for the less gifted. I think this has brought vocational training into disrepute in many communities of this nation. I hope that through this legislation vocational training will reach new heights of acceptability by the people of the provinces of this country.

I think we desperately need technicians. We must forget the idea that a technician is a second grade engineer, or an engineer that did not make good. As the hon. member suggested, too often we have people with engineering degrees doing jobs which could be done by technicians. This is an area where the Soviet union has completely surpassed us in education. This is an area where we must catch up. Particularly I hope that this is going to be a step toward a whole new concept as to what the federal government must do through grants, not to control all education but without endangering the autonomy of the provinces to provide assistance to education and training on a scale that will allow every person in this country to attain the height of achievement of which he is capable.

It has been suggested by the dominion bureau of statistics that over the next number of years we will need ten major universities in this country, not all centred in the larger communities but some also in smaller communities. I think one of the unfortunate aspects is that our university education is centred in the large metropolitan areas. In an area like my own, Peterborough, we have people who are desperately trying to set up a junior college. They need help.

This is also a whole new step toward the opening up of a whole new vista of federal assistance and motivation in the area of education because if we wish to make our educational system as good as it must be in the latter part of the twentieth century we need not only technicians and craftsmen but also economists, historians, philosophers and theologians. We need these as well. Let us not provide technicians and discover that the whole meaning of our western civilization has
Vocational Training
disappeared because we forgot that vocational training was only a part of our educational process.
Finally, it must be integrated somehow into a planned economy, and here again I hope, as the hon. member suggested, that the productivity council will come into play.

I wish the hon. member for Bow River were in his seat because I should like to answer the questions he asked a few nights ago when he inquired about the position of the new party in relation to socialism and free enterprise. I would suggest that we have stopped fighting the issue of socialism with a capital ""S"" and free enterprise with capitals ""F"" and ""E"". I am sure the hon. member realizes we live in a mixed economy and that the new party believes that the public sector as well as the private sector has rights, duties and responsibilities.

I was a little bit surprised at his method of attack by reading the words of leaders in this house some 30 years ago. I do not think there is any form of argument that is more historically suspect and academically unacceptable than wrenching from context words uttered 30 years ago.

2080352,ca.proc.d.1960-12-02.19.13,1960-12-02,a51b971d-def8-4a0a-bb73-d7116425be67,ca.m.2057,Mr. Horner (Jasper-Edson):,,I960,,,We have just heard a new definition of socialism. I thought when listening to the hon. member that what he gave us really sounded just like a schoolteacher's definition. However, now that we have this new party definition we can have both free enterprise and socialism together. Unfortunately, this is not true. This is just the socialist's way of gaining power, and then the rest of the restrictions of individual freedom have to come into play, because this is the only way the socialists can operate a planned economy, by having complete stat-ism, and it does not really matter very much whether you call it socialism, communism, or anything else. It means a complete lack of individual freedom and, as such, no longer do we have a free world or a free country.

I suggest to the hon. member that this measure is brought forward not as a part of a planned economy but as a plan on the part of a dynamic government to provide opportunity for all Canadians. So far as I am concerned, there are a few points I should like to touch on briefly. They have been touched on by a previous speaker, but I should like to bring to your attention, sir, the question of decentralization of the schools.

In my area in Alberta particularly, we are concerned and have been concerned not about the importation of European skilled workers but of United States skilled workers in the oil and gas and the pipe line industries. We are now on the verge of terrific expansion in our area with regard to natural gas and the processing plants and extraction plants that go along with it. Very recently I visited one in the Pembina field at the town of Drayton Valley and talked to the young people there who are running these plants. All of them were studying by correspondence and were receiving on the job training under supervision. This was one of the first plants in operation in Alberta and we have several others. We have another one in the Jumping Pound field in southern Alberta and construction is just going to start on another one in the Windfall field in my constituency. There will be a series of these gas extraction and processing plants throughout Alberta.
We are concerned about these plants being manned by United States technicians because

we do not have trained personnel in Canada. I should like to put it on the record that I hope the province of Alberta will take advantage of this program to establish immediately a technical school devoted to the oil and gas industry. In that regard I suggest to them that the town of Drayton Valley would be an ideal location for such a school as it offers all the on the job training required and is centrally located among the major gas and oil fields in the province.

I wish to put another point on the record with regard to the question of decentralization and I should like to quote from the report of the Cameron royal commission on education in the province of Alberta. In this regard they came to this conclusion:
That the scope of educational offerings at public expense in the public school system be broadened to include appropriate courses in many vocational areas.

They went on to suggest that this should be done by a program that would promote and develop community colleges specializing in the particular line which had to do with the raw materials or natural resources of the area. This is why I bring up the question of the oil and gas industry and a technical school in the town of Drayton Valley which is in the centre of the largest oil field in North America.

I wish to refer to one or two other aspects of vocational training and I should like to deal first with forestry. The provincial government recently established a school of forestry at Hinton which so far is under the direction of the department of lands and forests of the province. However, I hope they will see fit to convert it into an educational institution devoted to producing technicians for the forest industry, an institution which would serve northwestern Alberta and part of British Columbia as well.

There is another matter in which I have been interested for a great number of years as a result of my experience many years ago when I served on a town council. From what I can observe there is a great need right across Canada for trained municipal, town and city officials, employees with some training in municipal, provincial and federal law and with some elementary training in bookkeeping. I suggest to the authorities that this might be a field for the establishment of a technical school devoted to the training of municipal officials. In my view it would be a real step forward from the point of view of providing jobs and also providing improved and more efficient administration of our municipalities, towns and cities.
There is one other question I want to raise and it is one I have brought up before in the house on numerous occasions. It has to

do with veterinary medicine. We in western Canada are still hopefully waiting for a school of veterinary medicine. I suggest that perhaps the province could tie in with such a school a program of technical training to produce the technicians required in veterinary medicine and all other aspects of animal husbandry.

Although I realize this may be a provincial responsibility, I believe that if we are going to remain free we have to do more than just provide a technical education for our people, and in this regard I should like to quote from the Cameron commission minority report:

A school that furnishes only a narrow, vocational, workaday training to children of humble parentage is effectually denying the innate dignity of man, a doctrine which asserts that every individual, whatever his trade or his income, is entitled to share in the high, humane tradition of the liberal arts and sciences.

This latter is I think an effective answer to the speech of the hon. member for Peterborough. Most of what he had to say was good until he started to talk about a planned economy and the area in which he would have the government take control. The fallacy of the thinking of the socialists or the new party, if their new program is one of half free enterprise and half socialism, is that these things cannot work together any more than they can take one section of the public, as they are trying to do by taking the labouring class, and make a political party out of them for the purposes, I suspect, of the people who are directing the labour unions rather than for the good of the ordinary working man.

I believe that any person wishing to make his way in this world must first of all prepare himself with some specialized know-how by means of which to handle a particular job. Vocational Training

specified categories of persons will include young farmers and young city dwellers. There should be some provision for night classes for students of all ages. They might not consist of any more than 5 per cent of the total enrollment at a school but they would benefit greatly from technical and vocational training.

I was on the Eden Valley Indian reserve last fall and the need for vocational training among these Indians was forcibly brought to my attention. It was performed even by our forefathers in pioneer days but it seems as though it has not been one of those skills which the Indian has acquired. I have given considerable thought to the question of technical and vocational training schools. 2080362,ca.proc.d.1960-12-02.20.1.1,1960-12-02,ba1f4916-0b63-4654-9f27-242c3d276e6e,ca.m.6904,Mr. Frank Howard (Skeena) moved,,CANADA FAIR EMPLOYMENT PRACTICES ACT,AMENDMENT TO EXTEND APPLICATION TO CIVIL SERVICE,,the second reading of Bill No. C-9, to amend the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act (crown bound).

He said: Mr. Speaker, my remarks on the introduction of this particular bill will be quite few, because the contents of it are rather short and need no extensive introduction. I think the proposed principle is clear and well established. Also, we had a debate lasting an hour on a bill of a similar nature during the last session.

Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, I should say this. The Canada Fair Employment Practices Act which came into force in the summer of 1953-in July, I believe it was-contains the provision, in brief form, that an employer shall not discriminate against employees or potential employees in so far as race, national origin, colour or religion is concerned. It also provides that a trade union shall not

discriminate against potential or present members, nor shall it expel members on the ground or for the reason of race, national origin, colour or religion. The act also sets out certain procedures for the enforcement of its provisions and certain penalties if the act is contravened. Those parts are not germane to this particular bill but are only by way of an aside in this introduction.

We know it is not possible to legislate for a state of mind. Yet it is good to have on the statute books something of this nature that is an anti-discrimination statute, that protects individuals from discrimination because of race, colour, national origin, and so on. It tends to promote the cessation or the lessening of any acts of discrimination that may be based upon those factors that I mentioned earlier.

Perhaps I may read very briefly from section 3 of the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act-which this bill seeks to amend- in order that hon. members should understand how this act applies now. Section 3 reads:

This act applies to and in respect of employment upon or in connection with any work, undertaking or business that is within the legislative authority of the parliament of Canada, including, but not so as to restrict the generality of the foregoing-

Then it sets out a number of things to which it applies. Section 3 (m) is the relevant passage to which I wish to refer, namely: the employment by any corporation established to perform any function or duty on behalf of the government of Canada of employees.

This means that Canadian National Railways, T.C.A., the atomic energy commission, Polymer and the like are covered by this particular act and shall not engage in any of the practices that the present act prohibits.

The purpose of the bill before us is to extend the application of the provisions of the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act to the crown and to the employees of the crown; or, in effect, Her Majesty in right of Canada and the servants and agents of Her Majesty in right of Canada.

One of the principles behind proposing this bill, from our point of view, is that employees in the public service of Canada should be treated substantially the same as employees in private industry in Canada. By that I do not wish to imply that they should be treated as they have been within the last few days by this parliament because of the bill with which we have just dealt. But in general terms they should come into the same set of legislative provisions and regulations in so far as employee-employer relationships are concerned.
I am quite sure, and there is no shadow of a doubt in my mind-and I am sure there
Vocational Training

is no shadow of a doubt in the mind of anyone in this house-that the intent of the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act is followed by the civil service commission in its function of employing people. I am also quite sure that no discrimination exists on these bases whatsoever.

We had some discussion last session. A number of hon. members participated in the debate and raised a number of questions. Perhaps I might briefly deal with those questions at this time. One question raised was whether there might be an inconsistency in applying the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act to the provisions of the Civil Service Act or the regulations made thereunder.

Last year I undertook to check by telephone-and again this year I undertook to check by telephone-with the civil service commission to ascertain whether there existed in the Civil Service Act or in any of the regulations pursuant to it any reference to non-discrimination. I was told that there was no such reference in the act or regulations at the moment. I inquired further and was told that in 1942 there appeared on one of the old employment questionnaires to be completed by potential employees a reference to the colour of the individual, but that this did not now exist.

I was unable to determine just when the transitional point took place, when the reference to colour was eliminated from the questionnaires. I was told that it had existed in 1942 but does not exist at the moment and has not for some time.

I expect this year, if last session's activities are to be followed through, we will be having committees and we will have presented, I presume, a revised civil service bill. I assume that at the behest of the government it will be referred to a special committee of the house. Perhaps it would be appropriate this year for this particular bill now before us to receive endorsation and second reading, because I am certain that every hon. member supports the basic principle behind it. I think the bill should receive second reading at this stage and be referred to this special committee in order that the committee can study the Civil Service Act and the proposed changes thereto. The parliament of Canada, affirming that the Canadian nation is founded upon principles that acknowledge the supremacy of God, the dignity and worth of the human person and the position of the family in a society of free men and free institutions:

column2: the right of the individual to life, liberty, security of the person and enjoyment of property, and the right not to be deprived thereof except by due process of law;

column1: I submit that ""liberty"" must include the right of employment. Liberty must include the right to make a livelihood without discrimination based on race, religion, national origin, colour or sex.

Nasserden (Rosihern):,,CANADA FAIR EMPLOYMENT PRACTICES ACT,AMENDMENT TO EXTEND APPLICATION TO CIVIL SERVICE,,Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this discussion this afternoon on Bill No. C-9, my first reaction in examining the bill is that the explanation takes up a greater portion of the printed material than does the actual wording of the bill. I believe I should put on the record the explanatory notes which read as follows:
The purpose of this bill is to prevent discrimination by the government of Canada against its employees or applicants for employment in the public service.
The act presently applies as follows:

3. This act applies to and in respect of employment upon or in connection with any work, undertaking or business that is within the legislative authority of the parliament of Canada, including, but not so as to restrict the generality of the foregoing.

ferries between any province and any other province or between any province and any country other than Canada;

such works or undertakings as, although wholly situate within a province, are before or after their execution declared by the parliament of Canada to be for the general advantage of Canada or for the advantage of two or more of the provinces; and

employers engaged in any such work, undertaking or business;

column1: If I understand correctly the purpose of this bill it is to extend to those engaged in the civil service of Canada the benefits that are presently enjoyed by people in other walks of life. It is also my understanding that the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act now encompasses the employees of crown corporations but not the employees of the civil service.

This bill appears to anticipate something that will be coming before parliament in the not too distant future. Reference was made by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Broome) to the forthcoming revision of the Civil Service Act. It might be said that the passage of this bill would not in any way change what might take place at a later time in regard to that act that will be considered at a later date but I submit there is a difference-and it may be a shade of a difference-between the ordinary employees in Canada and those employed by the government of this country. That fact is borne out by some of the provisions now contained in the Civil Service Act.

I refer first of all to the preference to veterans, an association of ideas which I believe Canadians in all parts of the country want to see maintained because of the unequalled contribution that has been made to the preservation of the freedom of Canada by those who have served in the Canadian armed forces, a freedom extending not only to these individuals themselves but to Canadians in all walks of life.

Coupled with that premise, of course, is the other premise relating to those provisions incorporated into the Civil Service Act having to do with the problem of security. The problem of ideological warfare-if you want

to call it that-the clash of ideas from one end of the globe to the other certainly makes every one of us here in the House of Commons and I believe everyone in Canada stop to think when he considers some of the positions that must be held by the people in the employ of the government of this country. It may be said that this is discrimination but I think Canadians in general will agree that it is one of the things necessary for the preservation of our way of life and of the sovereignty of this nation.

I notice that this bill was brought forward last year and discussed' in January and February. No doubt hon. members are familiar with the discussion that took place at that particular time. As I read to you, sir, the provisions that this bill would provide I could not help but ask myself the question: Are any of those provisions already provided for Canadians by virtue of the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act and the provisions that were brought forward last year in the bill of rights, that bill which more than any other was so long overdue in this parliament.

When people talk of discrimination they mention, of course, discrimination in so far as race, colour and religion are concerned. Sometimes there are other forms of discrimination as well. Generally speaking, Canada is free from these types of discrimination. In fact, it would be difficult to put your finger in a substantive way on any particular case at any particular time. There have been times in the past, of course, particularly during wartime, when acts of parliament and decisions of the government have made necessary in the ordinary deliberations of parliament the passing of certain statutes which seemed to have caused a certain measure of discrimination; but, generally speaking, in most instances, those acts were passed for the preservation of freedom in this country, and as such were accepted by Canadian citizens in good faith.

Because of the fact that Canada is reasonably free from this type of discrimination, because of the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act as it stands today, because of the bill of rights, because of the examination of the Civil Service Act, which will be brought forward later on in this session, I cannot help but feel that this bill serves no useful purpose at this particular time in our deliberations and for that reason, I thought that I should voice those expressions of opinion so that other hon. members might judge for themselves as well.

Browne (Vancouver-Kingsway):,,CANADA FAIR EMPLOYMENT PRACTICES ACT,AMENDMENT TO EXTEND APPLICATION TO CIVIL SERVICE,,Mr. Speaker, with the statement that is contained in the explanatory notes of this bill to the effect that the purpose of this bill is

to prevent discrimination by the government of Canada against its employees or applicants for employment in the public service, I think everyone would agree. Of course, if any case was brought forward to substantiate the claim that there was any such discrimination I am sure we would want to take immediate action to prevent it. However, in this particular case the mover of the bill has stated that to his knowledge there is no such discrimination. Of course, that relieves us of the necessity of taking immediate action.

In view of the fact that the civil service is not generally covered in the same legislation as the rest of our labour force and has not been throughout the years, it is obviously a matter that needs a good deal of consideration. The Civil Service Act, of course, has been set up to deal with employees in the public service, and I think it has been generally conceded throughout the years that public servants have responsibilities and conditions different from those of other employees in the country. Many things have been put in the Civil Service Act to protect those employees, and there are certain advantages that they have enjoyed throughout the years that other employees have not had. Therefore, I do not think we can just accept the statement that everybody should be brought under the same legislation.

As has already been pointed out in connection with this bill, if it were passed it would bring the civil servants under the control of two different bodies. It would have the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) responsible for part of their activities and the civil service commission responsible for another part.

As I have already pointed out, with the study being made of the whole position of the civil service I think it would be unwise to make such a change at this time. I think in the Civil Service Act there are ample safeguards at the present time to prevent discrimination in the civil service. In chapter 48 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, section 19, the following appears:

Except where otherwise expressly provided, all appointments to the civil service shall be upon competitive examination under and pursuant to this act, and shall be during pleasure; but no appointment, whether permanent or temporary, shall be made to a local position within a province, and no employee shall be transferred from a position in a province to a local position in the same or in another province, whether permanent or temporary, until and unless the candidate or employee has qualified, by examination,-
Then, in section 25 we find:
(1) Competitive examinations shall be held by the commission to establish lists of persons eligible for appointment.
Vocational Training

(2) Such examinations may be written or oral or in the form of a demonstration of skill or any combination of these, and they shall be of a character fairly to test and determine the relative fitness and ability of candidates actually to perform the duties of the class to which they seek to be appointed, and any investigation of training and experience and any test of technical knowledge, manual skill, or physical fitness that, in the judgment of the commission, serves to this end may be employed.

In that way the examinations are open to everyone, and that in itself provides an adequate guarantee that everybody is going to have a fair opportunity of employment in the civil service. However, as has been pointed out, there are some advantages given for employment in the civil service by way of war veterans' preference. I would not be surprised to see proposed the suggestion that there should be other preference given. My own feeling is that perhaps we should specify that a preference should be given to Canadian citizens. I do not think that that would be an unwarranted preference, and yet under the terms of this proposed amendment it may well be that the power to have people given that preference may be taken out of our hands.

The bill of rights has already been referred to on several occasions, and that is another guarantee that there is going to be fairness in the application of the act. However, I have another reason for believing that the civil service should not some within the scope of the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act, because I believe there are other amendments that need to be made to that act and that perhaps the civil service should not necessarily come within the scope of those kinds of amendments.

For this reason I believe it would be very unwise to proceed with this amendment at this time. I should like to be able to deal with some of the other amendments that I feel should be made to the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act but I fear, Mr. Speaker, that you would rule me out of order at this time so I shall save them for another occasion.

2080382,ca.proc.d.1960-12-02.20.1.21,1960-12-02,eb1f264f-a92e-4bc5-a5da-0ac8c84dbd5c,ca.m.7239,Mr. Maclnnis:,,CANADA FAIR EMPLOYMENT PRACTICES ACT,AMENDMENT TO EXTEND APPLICATION TO CIVIL SERVICE,,Reference has been made to the bill of rights. I should like to point out that discrimination is completely guarded against under the bill of rights because in section 2 it is provided that every law of Canada shall, unless it is expressly declared by an act of the parliament of Canada that it shall operate notwithstanding the Canadian bill of rights, shall be so construed and applied as not to abrogate, etc., any rights or freedoms. Since the Civil Service Act comes under this jurisdiction this offers complete protection against discrimination on the ground of race, colour, creed or nationality.

The bill before us is an act to amend the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act and its chief purpose is to extend the act to bind Her Majesty in right of Canada and servants and agents of Her Majesty in right of Canada. At the present time crown corporations come within the ambit of the act. Section 3 of the act reads as follows:

This act applies to and in respect of employment upon or in connection with any work, undertaking or business that is within the legislative authority of the parliament of Canada, including, but not so as to restrict the generality of the foregoing.. .
(m) the employment by any corporation established to perform any function or duty on behalf of the government of Canada of employees.
That makes the act apply only to employees of Her Majesty in right of Canada.

The civil service commission has always followed a policy of non-discrimination and has never knowingly transgressed the principles laid down in the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act so far as race, colour or religion are concerned. Any differences in

treatment or application which can be attributed to race or origin have been imposed by the requirements of the provisions of the Civil Service Act. The civil service commission has revised its application forms from time to time to delete or modify questions of a nature incompatible with the provisions of the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act as applied to employees in private industry. This was done because of the close, informal working relations between the Department of Labour and the civil service commission with regard to the application of the principles of the act.

The Civil Service Act gives certain preferences to war veterans and residents of a locality in filling jobs in a particular area and also with respect to the admission to examination of British subjects with at least five years residence in Canada. From time to time, however, as the need arises the commission departs from the operation of the relevant section with respect to a position where it is necessary to admit to examination people who do not qualify in these respects.

The provisions of section 4 of the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act have to do with discrimination on the ground of race, colour or religion, and while it may be contended that in the case of British subjects there is special provision, the effect of the amendment would be to give the Minister of Labour authority to deal with complaints concerning discrimination in employment which in all other respects are subject to the Civil Service Act and the administration of the civil service commission. In view of this situation there could not conceivably be any conflict in the exercise of this authority.

The status given by the bill to the Minister of Labour and to the industrial inquiry commission appointed under the act would be repugnant to the Civil Service Commission reporting as it does solely to parliament and not being under the supervision or direction of any minister of the crown. As outlined, the policies and practices of the commission in protecting a person seeking employment or who is already employed in the public service from discrimination on the basis of national origin, colour, creed or religion, are based upon the application of the principles employed in the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act, the Civil Service Act or otherwise.

I know that from time to time the commission has revised its application forms to delete or modify questions of a nature considered incompatible with the provisions of the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act as applied to employers in private industry. I understand that there are provisions in

the Civil Service Act or the regulations made thereunder that are applicable to appointments to the civil service in relation to residence, security, or citizenship which might be inconsistent with the literal application of the amendment to the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act proposed in the bill.

In view of the considerations referred to it might be deemed preferable that the purpose of the bill should be given effect to under the Civil Service Act rather than under the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act. This consideration is particularly pertinent at this time when legislation for the enactment of a new Civil Service Act is projected for the present session of parliament.

,,,Malcolm MacInnis,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=eb1f264f-a92e-4bc5-a5da-0ac8c84dbd5c&Language=E&Section=ALL

Phillips (Prince):,,CANADA FAIR EMPLOYMENT PRACTICES ACT,AMENDMENT TO EXTEND APPLICATION TO CIVIL SERVICE,,Mr. Speaker, it is very easy to be sympathetic to the principle of the bill but I lost a certain amount of sympathy for the bill when the hon. member who introduced it stated that there was no discrimination in the government service and he did not intend to imply that there was. In fact, as recorded in Hansard last year when he introduced a similar bill he made an almost identical speech and in it he emphasized that he knew of no case of discrimination. I think that the bill would have had a great deal more emphasis if he had been able to show cause for its introduction.

I do not mean to imply that discrimination does not exist anywhere in Canada. Periodically we read of extremely unfortunate situations. These may or may not be valid cases of discrimination. However, I am quite sure that the hon. member will not find discrimination either in the civil service or in the crown corporations.

The civil service commission established by law, clearing any government department and reporting directly to parliament rather than through a minister, go to great effort in order to avoid discrimination. They have certain preferences, however. I am sure that all hon. members have received complaints with regard to those preferences. I know that periodically I get complaints from people in the 20-25 age bracket who say that they lost out in a civil service competition owing to the veterans' preference. I think perhaps they have a certain justification for their complaints in that they say they were not old enough to enlist in any of the services during wartime and get the benefits of the Civil Service Act with regard to overseas preference. On the other hand, I do not think the average Canadian considers this to be discrimination and I think he would want the veterans' preference maintained. A number of people have approached me and wanted to know why the preference could not be

extended to those with handicaps. In small towns in Canada it is quite difficult to obtain employment for a handicapped person. They feel that they should have a certain preference under the Civil Service Act.

2080457,ca.proc.d.1960-12-02.33.5.7,1960-12-02,d3117809-e7d1-45d2-9762-d1a2621aa271,ca.m.3975,Mr. Speaker:,Speaker of the House of Commons,EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,PROVISION FOR CONTINUANCE OF RAILWAY OPERATIONS,,Before putting the motion I must determine whether there is a prima facie question of privilege, and I shall be glad to hear hon. members on that point. A motion based on privilege must be founded on a finding by the Chair that there is a question of privilege. I think there is a proper question of privilege in that if, as is asserted and as appears to be the case, the Hansard report of the final stages of the proceedings of the committee is incorrect, that is a matter that the house will be concerned with as a breach of its privilege to have its proceedings correctly reported.

However, the consequences which the hon. member for Skeena suggests do not appear to me to be self-evident, because what in fact ensued was that the chairman reported the bill as amended and the house itself adopted the report of the committee which was a report of the amended bill without reservation or limitation. If there was an irregularity in the proceedings of the committee that irregularity, it seems to me, is cured by the action of the house itself. Therefore the suggestion made by the hon. member for Skeena appears to me, without opportunity for further reflection, not to follow from the omission which was made in committee.

On the other hand, the incorrect report in Hansard is a matter which I think the house very properly has a duty to take into account. Whether the hon. member, in view of what I have said, wishes me to proceed with this motion is a matter for him to decide.

Winch (Vancouver East):,,EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,PROVISION FOR CONTINUANCE OF RAILWAY OPERATIONS,,Mr. Speaker, on this occasion of third reading of this very important bill I would like to say a few words and take a few minutes' time on behalf of our group in this House of Commons.

We recognize very completely the importance and seriousness of the problem which is facing this country and this house, and the difficulties that arise. We recognize- and all hon. members have stated this- the effect that a cessation of work in the transportation industry could have, not only on those directly involved but those who would be indirectly affected as Canadian citizens engaged in other operations in our Canadian economy.

A great deal has been said both pro and con in these last few days on the legislation which is now before us. 1 think the position of our group has been made exceedingly clear. We regret that matters should have come to a position where the introduction of such legislation was deemed necessary by the government. We have pointed out that in our opinion, had there not been delayed action by the government it should have been possible, among responsible government, responsible employers and responsible employees, to work out a satisfactory solution. We feel most strongly-and we have demonstrated this by word and by vote up to this time-that in the introduction of the legislation the government has not taken what we consider a fair approach or an unbiased attitude. We in this group, sir, cannot accept in principle the introduction of legislation which will remove from a segment of the workers of this country an inalienable right ^yaXan ky law and given to most, because of the failure of government, employers and employees to work out a satisfactory solution.

Very briefly, we feel it is wrong. We cannot endorse the removal of a right, in particular in an industry which is very strongly regulated by government, when there is a majority report and when it must be admitted by all fair men upon due consideration that the 110,000 employees affected now have a gap, I believe, of around 29 cents an hour compared with the standard which has been generally accepted; that is, compared with those employed in the durable goods industries.
We feel that on almost every ground of principle affecting the rights of these workers, their positions and their standards, the government is really remiss in the manner in
which the legislation has been introduced_______
or should I say in what is left out of the legislation as far as the employees are concerned.

The government is asking, through the medium of this legislation, for the removal of what should be inalienable rights. As the law is going to be amended at this time, these rights will be removed. These employees, having carried on in a responsible manner now for over a year, are being asked

Maintenance of Railway Operation Act to continue tor another six months with no change in their standards and with no remedial action to close the gap between the standards which have been accepted for many years. In particular, Mr. Speaker, we cannot see how, with the passage of this legislation there will be a different position on May 15 of next year. In other words, we are going to have a continuous period of anxiety for just over six months, and then perhaps we will have to face the identical situation which we are facing at the present time.

We think that is unfortunate. There is nothing in the legislation, and nothing has been said by the government, that can possibly lead us to any conclusion other than that this is merely a policy-wise move, a stall, hoping that something may happen in the next six months. The Prime Minister stated what will most likely occur before May 1; that is, a lifting of the freight rate freeze, which I think undoubtedly must involve the question of whether there will be a continuation of the subsidy as far as freight rates are concerned. That is a situation, sir, which is almost untenable when you look at it today and try to look forward to what the situation will be on May 15. It is these reasons, amplified in the two days' discussion, that we felt had to be mentioned on the motion for third reading of this bill.

But, Mr. Speaker, there is one point that disturbs us greatly and it is this. As the legislation now stands-definitely as the legislation now stands-and considering anything expressed by the Prime Minister or the Minister of Labour, there is nothing to indicate that there will be any differentiation between now and six months from now. This can only lead to what I term a period of anxiety for the employees directly or indirectly affected. We feel that something should be placed in the legislation itself which would indicate that there was a possibility of removing the cause of this anxiety in the next six months, that this should not be left to wishful thinking on the part of the Prime Minister or the Minister of Labour with the probability that we shall be facing a situation on May 15 similar to the one we are facing at the present time. In other words, we feel there should be some provision in the legislation to direct that between now and May 15, when this bill becomes inoperative, there shall be a continuation of negotiations.

We feel that both men and industry must be reasonable. I know that workers are reasonable, because few things are so unpleasant as being out of work. The Canadian economy, as well as the position in which the workers find themselves, demand the removal

of this period of six month's anxiety leading to a likely repetition of the present situation six or seven months from now. Although I personally regret very much the necessity of placing in legislation any provision to insist that responsible men should get together,

I do not feel, because of the importance of this question to the country's economy and to the workers involved, that we can afford to leave the situation up in the air. It is simply not good enough to rely on wishful thinking.
It is because we feel that this question is of major importance that I move, seconded by the hon. member for Skeena:
That Bill No. C-45 be not now read a third time but that it be referred back to the committee of the whole house for the purpose of reconsidering clause 3.

May I say in this regard that I should like to have mentioned more fully the purpose I have in mind, but there are certain rules of procedure; some things are in order and others are out of order. I know this is in order. I want the house to understand that the purpose of this amendment on third reading is to get the bill back into committee of the whole on clause 3 in order that the committee might give consideration to whether we should not give a legislative indication to the companies and to the employees that there is not to be a hiatus between now and May 15, and that the parties must get together as responsible people in an effort to work out a collective agreement before the expiry of a bill which is to become an act of parliament.

May I end by saying that we in this group are moving this amendment because we feel it is our responsibility as members of parliament to do so in the interests of the Canadian economy and of the Canadian workers who are directly or indirectly affected.

2080505,ca.proc.d.1960-12-02.33.5.55,1960-12-02,84909dc1-9a60-44b3-a939-2393ab563089,ca.m.3212,Mr. Diefenbaker:,Prime Minister,EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,PROVISION FOR CONTINUANCE OF RAILWAY OPERATIONS,,I have not belonged to that group. In 1950 I took a strong and firm stand-and have throughout the years- against that form of legislation.

It has been said by the hon. member for Vancouver East that there should be a continuation of the conciliation processes provided for in the legislation. At any time an agreement is arrived at, this legislation ceases to be effective. I want to see these people together. We brought them together; we endeavoured to ascertain whether there was any possibility of agreement. I have said, and I repeat, that there was not that attitude on the part of either that would bring about anything in the nature of an agreement, reasonable in its characteristics. The preamble of the bill reads:

Whereas the processes of collective bargaining between the major railway companies and the representatives of their non-operating employees have failed to produce agreement, and the public interest requires that further efforts to react
agreement be resumed at a more favourable time without prejudice to the rights of either party and without interruption of the railway service;
Further on, in paragraph 3, we find the following:

Subject to this act, the term of each existing collective agreement is extended to include the period beginning on the commencement of this act and ending on the day on which a new collective agreement between the parties thereto in amendment or revision thereof comes into effect.

This makes every provision for a continuation of the conciliation proceedings. More than that, I think these people should be brought together at once. We continue the railways in operation. I for one will do everything I can to bring them together and regularly call them together so as to assure that discussions will continue and that justice will be done. So far as unfairness to the employees is concerned, there can be no justification for any truculent attitude being taken toward them.

There is one thing that I must answer, namely the suggestion that we in any way had acted for the benefit of the C.P.R. On the one hand, it was said and repeated that the Canadian Pacific railway wanted a strike to put the men in their places. That has been repeated here on more than one occasion. It must have been asserted with knowledge or it would not have been asserted, although I have no knowledge of that fact. If that is so, this legislation is a most effective answer to those who say there was any relationship between the Canadian Pacific and the government in this regard, because the tragic results which would follow such an attitude shall not and will not be countenanced.

I want to underline and emphasize that once again. The suggestion that that railway company would endeavour to do this to the workers of this country is such an outrageous one that if it has any foundation in fact, we have met it by preserving completely and absolutely the rights of labour and assuring at the same time the operation of the railways.

As far as the Canadian National Railways management are concerned, while the government has no authority over them-it is a separate and independent organization, and any interference in any way would be immediately challenged as improper and unjustifiable-I want to make it perfectly clear that if the management of the railway does things that ought not to be tolerated, that will do injustice to the workers of this country, this government, while scrupulously maintaining independence of that railway, will

Maintenance of Railway Operation Act certainly have the attention of the management brought to any such unfairness or discrimination against any of the workers of that railway. I want that definitely understood.

It has been a trying problem, sir, for all of us. We have tried to discharge our responsibilities. We have recognized that there will be misinterpretation of what we have done; that there will be endeavours to take political advantage of the course of action, as though we were in fact freezing wages to the detriment of the worker. As I said, we will maintain the conciliation processes from now until May 15. Instead of fixing a date away beyond, we fixed it in May so there would be no unjustified prolongation of the problem. We will bring these people together from time to time. Then, as I pointed out before, as soon as the freight rate freeze is lifted we will be in a position to bring about measures such as the hon. member for Assiniboia said were necessary to remove injustices and discriminatory rates, as far as that can be achieved, and the railways will be in a position to proceed in the only way in which expenses can be paid, namely either by grants or subsidies from parliament, in which case it comes out of the people through taxation, or through freight rates, which means that the users must pay additional amounts because of the increased expenses of operation.

We say this, and I repeat; it has been a difficult problem. I think parliament in the action it will take or is taking, provided that this bill is passed, to bring about a period not of inaction but of continued discussion between the parties, is doing the right thing. I believe the voice of reason will be heard; that public opinion has a tremendous influence on the production, the generation and the maintenance of reasonable, good common sense. If not, when we lift the freeze we will give the assurance that those who are workers on the railways, with their unions representing them, will be able to present their case, and that whatever is substituted in the place of the present agreements will be retroactive in fact to January 1, 1960.

There is no prejudice; there is postponement in order to prevent a strike taking place. Instead of taking the other course and bringing in compulsory arbitration, as suggested by the opposition-that in effect is what they say-we took the course we believed to be reasonable, namely the maintenance inviolate of the rights of labour, at the same time maintaining the public interest and welfare of 17,500,000 other Canadians. I think that in the process of time, as this becomes apparent and the rights of both sides become clear in the perspective of the days
Maintenance of Railway Operation Act ahead, what we have done will turn out to have been the proper and, indeed, the only course, the course of reason and of common sense.

2080541,ca.proc.d.1960-12-02.33.5.91,1960-12-02,57dd42c2-427c-4252-9a45-f0c416cc0e1b,ca.m.5944,Mr. Pitman:,,EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,PROVISION FOR CONTINUANCE OF RAILWAY OPERATIONS,,-not to delay this legislation. My remarks will be brief and I hope, unemotional. However, at this point I would like to state the differences which exist between this group and the other parties in this house.

We believe, as do the other parties, that there should be no railway strike. We do not believe there should be any compulsion on workers to work at a wage level which has been found unacceptable by all standards and which would be unacceptable to any fair-minded Canadian. We do not believe that workers should be prepared to compromise themselves and compromise their fellow workers by doing so.

On the other hand, we do not believe that we in this house should legislate to the effect that management should pay, either. I think the Minister of Labour and the Prime Minister made a very good point when they suggested that there might be a time in the future when the house would be faced with similar legislation when the unions will have refused to accept a majority report of a conciliation board. On the other hand, I also accept the statement of the Leader of the Opposition
that he does not wish for an arbitrary solution. He believes there should be free play as between workers and management.

However, we believe that when parliament has to legislate in a situation such as this, neither labour nor management should be put at a disadvantage. That is why this group believe that if there is a national emergency the people of this nation would be willing to allow a favourable atmosphere to occur, an atmosphere in which neither management nor labour would be at a disadvantage. Here again, I think the former minister of transport had a good point when he called attention to the fact that this was an unusual situation because freight rates are frozen. By May 15 freight rates will be unfrozen and the royal commission report will have come down. At that time I am sure there will be a favourable atmosphere, because the workers will not be at a disadvantage and neither will management because they are not being obliged, through legislation, to pay higher wages.

I think this is the basis upon which a statesmanlike decision can be achieved. I think this is the basis upon which the citizens of Canada would be prepared to accept a subsidy until May 15 which, as the Prime Minister has pointed out, would amount to very little. On this basis I believe a change of atmosphere could occur immediately, a change which would bring together labour and management, and allow them to continue negotiations and, perhaps more than anything else, find a standard which would be acceptable and reasonable for the nonoperative railway workers, one which would be much higher than that suggested in the majority report of the conciliation board.

Fisher (Port Arthur):,,EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,PROVISION FOR CONTINUANCE OF RAILWAY OPERATIONS,,There are very few remarks I want to make now on this bill. It is not the practice for one opposition group to challenge another opposition group to explain its position, but there is one thing I do want to note. The prime point made by the Liberal-labour opposition, as I am going to call it, is that they possess a managerial concept which is peculiar and unique. This is the prime point they made in support of how they would handle this situation.

No one likes to be catty or nasty about these points, but I think we deserve an explanation of this managerial asset which the Liberal party has. I have looked around this chamber and I do not think the members of the Liberal party will be insulted if I say I do not see any managerial mystique right here. I can think of a number of names- Mitchell Sharp, Davidson Dunton, Bill Buchanan, Walter Gordon, Bob Fowler and
others-but they are not here, and we do not know whether they are part of this managerial concept, this shadow cabinet, which the Liberals have.

The hon. member for Essex East says, in complete sincerity I am sure, that the key point is that the Liberals would go ahead on 'sound principles'. This, again, is a part of the managerial conception.

What are these sound principles which are so basic and so unique to the Liberal party? I think what we shall have to do is accept, or anticipate, an argument on small ""1"" liberal principles, not large ""L"" Liberal party principles, because I am having a very difficult time seeing how this Liberal managerial concept makes any great contribution to this particular situation. I am not going to say the same things about the other points which the Leader of the Opposition brought up, because I think they were worth while, but he did lead off by talking about this managerial mystique nonsense. Of course I am biased, but I just cannot see this managerial ability which the Liberal party apparently supposes itself to possess at the present time. It is nothing but a social nostalgia on the part of the hon. gentleman; memories of C. D. and all that.

I think I can finish before one o'clock. In so far as the royal commission on transportation is concerned and some of the remarks made by the Prime Minister on television- the right hon. gentleman will correct me if I inadvertently misquote him-as I understand it the Prime Minister said on television that the royal commission had to a degree been delayed or held up by illness. I have checked this matter-

2080546,ca.proc.d.1960-12-02.33.5.96,1960-12-02,6e0e7dad-52e6-426d-b6d7-f3a4924ce2de,ca.m.7504,Mr. Fisher:,,EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,PROVISION FOR CONTINUANCE OF RAILWAY OPERATIONS,,The whole basis for this six months' delay until May 15 in the bill is the royal commission hearings. So far, the royal commission has not missed a single hearing that I know about due to illness. There has been illness of members, of course, and I understand that at the present time the chairman is not in as good physical condition as we might hope. I have here the last printed volume of the proceedings open at the 24,000 page mark, which surely indicates how extremely complicated this question is. I wish to underline the fact that this commission, by 90205-6-30|

Maintenance of Railway Operation Act the terms of this legislation, or at any rate by its implications, will be obliged to come up with a report by March 31, although it still has hearings called for January which may run into February.

This illustrates the pressure which is being placed on the royal commission as a result of this legislation, a pressure which is most unusual, especially when we recall that royal commissions have for generations been the butt of jokes founded on the length of time they take to make their reports. Hon. members may recall the legendary royal commission on kissing which, according to A. P. Herbert, was set up in 1874 and has not reported yet. This commission, however, has to get its work done in maybe three months, and by then it will have more than 25,000 pages of evidence. Thus I make the final point that this bill places a most unfair burden on the royal commissioners, people for whom, ordinarily, I have no great sympathy.

One of the points which have been brought to the attention of the royal commission throughout its hearings has been that the railways, in the last couple of years, have been reaping tremendous advantages throughout the years in productivity increases as a result of the introduction of new equipment. There has never been any discussion here as to how that relates to the present situation.
May I call it one o'clock?

2080549,ca.proc.d.1960-12-02.33.5.99,1960-12-02,6e0e7dad-52e6-426d-b6d7-f3a4924ce2de,ca.m.7504,Mr. Fisher:,,EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,PROVISION FOR CONTINUANCE OF RAILWAY OPERATIONS,,I want to make a point that the productivity increases have been immense. While it is true that the revenue of the railways has been frozen, the companies have had tremendous possibilities for saving. That is certainly the key to most of the western arguments before the royal commission. Surely this gives the railways the leeway to do something about better wages.

We have heard no argument raised on this particular point, but if I were a railway worker I know I would have in mind the development of central traffic control, the running of two divisions, greater productivity of diesels and new yards, and so on, because all this should put the companies in a better position. To argue from the operating revenues of the railway at this time is not nearly as relevant as to look at the costs.
I think this point should be underlined. The

Maintenance of Railway Operation Act workers in this case are working for a management that has had a decreasing scale of costs in terms of productivity as a result of innovations. This should be a strong factor in any consideration of wage rates for them.

2080554,ca.proc.d.1960-12-02.33.5.104,1960-12-02,0daa460f-b2c1-447e-abbe-c4bd1f237b32,ca.m.6630,Mr. Hazen Argue (Assiniboia):,,EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,PROVISION FOR CONTINUANCE OF RAILWAY OPERATIONS,,Mr. Speaker, before we take this vote, I should like very briefly to go over the main points of criticism and the main propositions that are being put forward by our group at this time.

Our first position is that this legislation should not have been necessary; that the government might have taken another course that would have solved the problem, and would not have placed parliament in the position of having to deal with legislation that we think is repugnant to the Canadian way of life, is undemocratic and should not be embarked upon by any free parliament except in a very extreme emergent situation, which we think did not need to arise.

We agree with all those who have said that everything possible should be done to avoid a strike; that a strike would bring difficulty perhaps chaos to many communities and industries in this country, and that management, workers and government should together have been able to bring forward a proposition that would have avoided a strike.

Beyond question there is compulsion in this bill. This is what the bill is about; it is to force the railway workers and the companies to maintain and continue operations until May 15. The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) said that this is not compulsory arbitration. He argues that after May 15 next year the parties will go back to their original position. In this legislation he has failed to give anything to the workers involved. The attitude of the Liberal party is that had there been in this legislation a provision for
compulsory arbitration along the lines of the legislation of 1950, they would have been in support of it.

2080557,ca.proc.d.1960-12-02.33.5.107,1960-12-02,0daa460f-b2c1-447e-abbe-c4bd1f237b32,ca.m.6630,Mr. Argue:,,EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,PROVISION FOR CONTINUANCE OF RAILWAY OPERATIONS,,The position of the Liberal party is that this kind of legislation with that provision added is something that they could support. We are opposed to this legislation, as we were opposed to the legislation in 1950. We are opposed to compulsion without arbitration; we are opposed to compulsion with arbitration. We feel that the workers have a good case. The Prime Minister has admitted it, the Liberal party in the house has stated it and we have stated it, and yet in this legislation nothing is being done to recognize that principle; and so the workers involved are exceedingly disappointed with what is now taking place.

I have said on a previous occasion that in our judgment the C.P.R. was in a financial position to meet the majority report of the conciliation board. However, it is understandable that the Canadian Pacific railway would dig in its heels and say no when they became aware that the government would bring about this kind of legislation which would remove the pressure that the workers had been able to place on the railways. The government assured the railway and the country that the company would continue operations even without an increase in wages, and therefore the company had nothing to lose.

We have suggested that, as an alternative to the compulsion in the bill presented by the government, as an alternative to the compulsion that the Liberal party is prepared to support, there is and there was another way out, where compulsion would not have been necessary, where the government might have taken action to resolve the problem in a way that would help the workers and the Canadian public. We suggested that a subsidy should be paid from the national treasury and that this subsidy at least from now on until May 15, and perhaps beyond that, would have removed the grievance of the workers and the opposition of the railway companies to signing an agreement. We think this was a reasonable proposition. The government will argue and does argue that a subsidy in this instance is wrong. The Liberal party is not prepared to support this kind of a subsidy. We suggest that a subsidy of this size for this purpose at this time is a much fairer way to deal with this question than the attitude taken by the government to force the men back to work and say that next May 15 our policy is to load the additional wages on to the freight users of this country.

What the Prime Minister has said is that a strike next spring may be possible. He said that the government is removing the right to strike at this time, not the right to strike in the future. The Prime Minister is saying that with the restoration of the rights of free men in this situation an application can then be made to the board of transport commissioners. As I see it, what will happen, what the government intends to happen, is a very large increase in freight rates next spring. It wants to bring about the postponement of the problem until then at which time the burden of the increase will be loaded on the freight service users of the country.

As a matter of fact, an additional part of their policy has become clear, namely that the subsidy now in effect for the purpose of maintaining freight rates as they exist will be withdrawn and the country will face a very large and, I am positive, discriminatory increase in freight rates because it is practically impossible to bring about a complete equality of all freight rates even though, as I have said, I have great confidence in M. A. MacPherson, the chairman of the royal commission.
We do not reject subsidies as part of a national policy. We think it is time for a general transportation policy that will provide parity of treatment to the workers.

,Co-operative Commonwealth Federation (C.C.F.),,Hazen Robert Argue,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=0daa460f-b2c1-447e-abbe-c4bd1f237b32&Language=E&Section=ALL
