2080559,ca.proc.d.1960-12-02.33.5.109,1960-12-02,0daa460f-b2c1-447e-abbe-c4bd1f237b32,ca.m.6630,Mr. Argue:,,EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,PROVISION FOR CONTINUANCE OF RAILWAY OPERATIONS,,Mr. Speaker, your admonition is, I think, fair. However, I think it is perfectly correct to say that the debate on third reading so far has been very wide ranging and reference has been made to many things far removed from the contents of the bill. I was about to say, and on this point I will conclude in a couple of sentences, that we have suggested that there should be a national transportation policy of which subsidies should be an integral part, a national transportation policy which will provide parity for the workers in the transport industry generally, which will provide equality of treatment and where any subsidy will be applied in a fair and equitable manner to the
Maintenance of Railway Operation Act railroads, air lines, truck transport companies and the workers who make their living in all of these various branches of the transportation industry.

I think one of the reasons for the impasse today is the hodgepodge that has developed over the years in our transportation industry. We are suggesting in this amendment that the house should once again give consideration to the proposition that particular provision should be made for the continuation of conciliation procedures in the hope that the railway companies and the workers may yet come to an agreement. I think the amendment before the house is based upon a very desirable objective. We are disappointed that the Liberal opposition has decided to vote against it but nevertheless we think it is a good proposition.

,Co-operative Commonwealth Federation (C.C.F.),,Hazen Robert Argue,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=0daa460f-b2c1-447e-abbe-c4bd1f237b32&Language=E&Section=ALL
2080560,ca.proc.d.1960-12-02.33.5.110,1960-12-02,5996b081-97f6-4bde-8dec-52df3dca3f76,ca.m.9560,Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Bonavisla-Twillin-gate):,,EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,PROVISION FOR CONTINUANCE OF RAILWAY OPERATIONS,,Mr. Speaker, before the vote is taken I should like to correct a misstatement that the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) made-I do not accuse him of being intentional about this-with respect to the position of the Liberal party. As I heard him say it, he said that this legislation would be acceptable to the Liberal party if it provided for compulsory arbitration. That, of course, is completely wrong.

What the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) said this morning was that this legislation would be acceptable to the Liberal party if it was amended to impose the terms recommended in the majority report of the conciliation board. That is not arbitration but rather a determination by parliament which is a very different thing. We are concerned with an agreement that expired on December 31, 1959 and is only continued in operation by the general law, and under the bill we are determining that that shall be the agreement. We think that if we are going to impose settlement by parliament, and that is what the government is asking us to do, the settlement imposed by parliament should be one that was determined independently to be fair. That is our position.

The government is asking parliament to compel the men to stay at work, and we support that, but the government is also compelling the men to stay at work at wages that the men refuse to regard as fair and reasonable, and we do not support that. We think, as the Leader of the Opposition said, that if you are going to compel the men to stay at work the companies should be compelled to pay between now and next May the amounts determined in the majority award, that there should be no subsidy now but that next May or June or whenever it is-here we differ completely with the C.C.F.-a general review

Maintenance of Railway Operation Act be made after the report of the royal commission, which we do not think should be prejudged and any disability to the railways resulting from this imposition should then be taken into account in the policy determined by parliament. That is the position we take.

We are not suggesting that in this case there should be compulsory arbitration. There is nothing to arbitrate. There are two positions. The companies say that they do not want to pay anything more. The men say that they are satisfied with the majority award. When I said there was nothing to arbitrate I was perhaps wrong. An arbitration would involve the determination of something in between these two positions. That is what an arbitration would do. We are not in favour of arbitration. BENIDICKSON    REFERENCE TO SPEECH OF MINISTER OF LABOUR,,,Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege which I think affects all hon. members of the house and which will certainly prove to affect the privileges of many outside the house.

Your Honour will appreciate our unusual difficulty today in that we sat until about two o'clock this morning and that was followed by an early morning sitting today. In consequence of this I was not able to look at my own Hansard until a few moments ago. I do not have the privileges of many others in the house who concurrent with the sittings of the house are supplied with blue sheets from Hansard.

I refer Your Honour to page 398 of Hansard of December 1 where the remarks of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) appear. I was aware at that time that I would likely shortly follow the minister who was concluding the debate on second reading and in consequence thereof I made very close notes of some of the pertinent remarks he was making. I made careful notes and I still have those notes in my hand. I find that in the first paragraph of his remarks yesterday he referred to ""the best possible way"" which I have here in quotation marks. In the second paragraph of his speech on page 398 in the left hand column I find to my surprise that he is reported to have said in that paragraph:
The purpose of this bill is to extend the present agreements to May 15 and to give the opportunity for collective bargaining-

At that point for the purposes of reply, as I indicated, I made notes. I distinctly heard the minister say that there would be given the opportunity after May 15 to strike. There is nothing in the text today that has reference to the words ""opportunity after May 15 to strike"". To establish that was elementary to my remarks during the course of the debate.

If Your Honour will look at the next page 400, in the right hand column, you will find that this subject also interested the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin). The hon. member for Essex East was questioning the minister as to the rights of the workers after May 15. In the right hand column on that page the hon. member for Essex East is reported as having said:
The government has said that all it is doing is postponing the situation. What will happen on May 15 if the men decide to strike?
I intervened at that point and said:
The minister has already said he will give them the opportunity to strike on May 15.
Questions of Privilege

I know that some ministers who, as I say, are supplied with blue sheets from Hansard and do not have to go to the debates office on the third floor as some of the rest of us do, occasionally have the assistance of their staff-their secretaries or executive assistants-in the revision of their Hansard text. I should like the minister to indicate to the house whether he personally made any elimination of the phrase I read from my notes or if not whether he would inquire and ascertain if any member of his staff made a correction in the Hansard text differing from the note I have outlined?

2080624,ca.proc.d.1960-12-02.39.1.1.1,1960-12-02,,,,stagedirection,,,,The house resumed, from Friday, November 25, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Starr-Mr. Flynn in the chair:

That it is expedient to introduce a measure to authorize the Minister of Labour to enter into agreements with provincial governments for the encouragement of technical and vocational training and to authorize the making of contributions by Canada toward the cost of programs of technical and vocational training undertaken under provincial

authority, including contributions toward the cost of capital expenditures on training facilities connected with such programs; to authorize the Minister of Labour to undertake programs of technical and vocational training for specified categories of persons; to provide for the establishment and operation of an advisory council and the appointment of its members and staff and to define its duties; and to provide for other related and incidental matters.

2080625,ca.proc.d.1960-12-02.39.1.2,1960-12-02,3c7abf33-5a24-4c46-87e9-5a6c9d457af5,ca.m.9967,Mr. Caron:,,VOCATIONAL TRAINING,PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL PROGRAMS,,"Mr. Chairman, a week ago I had to interrupt my remarks at the sounding of the six o'clock bell announcing the adjournment of the house. At that time I was saying that since the beginning of the session the government has suggested amendments to some acts that were already in our statutes, but without saying so forthright, leading us to believe that entirely new bills were being introduced.

As a matter of fact, in the resolution under consideration, there is only one thing different from the act of 1952 and the amendments of 1954, and that is the establishment of an advisory council, and nothing else. Now, we urge the government to consult with the provinces with a view to ensuring a more adequate training to those who are about to start on their own, and those who are already on the labour market and must change jobs when they are not completely ready to do so, especially day labourers. But the department should have entered into negotiations with the province before introducing this legislation. Because we know that education at all levels, comes under provincial jurisdiction. Now, suppose we pass the bill that will follow the resolution under discussion, what will happen if the provinces, not having been consulted, say no for some reason or other? We would have passed a totally ineffective bill.

With regard to the field of education, I wonder if French-Canadian members from the province of Quebec would like to make their opinion known to us, because we all know how they objected to the intervention of the federal government in this field. They have done so repeatedly since 1953, or since the Liberal government decided to assist universities. How can they agree to vote for such legislation today?

I probably could have asked the Secretary of State (Mr. Dorion) if he would care to make again the speeches he used to make before he accepted the joint responsibility of the cabinet, but I would not dare. I should like, however, that some Quebec member
Vocational Training

state his stand and that of his colleagues on this resolution. As for us, our mind is at rest. The Liberals have accepted and recognized that the federal government had the right to interfere in the field of education, in so far as the provinces agreed, and we shall pursue that course.

The present project is a long range one and we intend to endorse it. We recognize that its purpose is to prepare, in a rather distant future, the young generation so that it might play its part within society. But what is being done at the present time? Has the Department of Labour found a way to settle the present economic emergency, when thousands of workers seek employment and thousands of unemployed are unable to withdraw unemployment insurance benefits because they lack the required number of stamps?

Are we able to find, in this resolution, anything which might relieve the immediate plight? Even though I studied every resolution on the order paper, I found nothing which could remedy the present plight of our society.

We are all in favour of long term assistance projects, but we maintain that the government has the responsibility of trying to settle the immediate problem of those who are suffering from unemployment in spite of what the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) had promised, of those who do not have enough bread on their table or enough money to pay their rent and who have to ask the municipalities for help through direct relief.

At this time, the government is following the policy it has adopted in the past, which means that it is passing on its responsibility to the municipalities. Long term legislation can be proposed similar to that which we now have for consideration and which will take one, two or even three years to give results, but in the meantime the municipalities have to bear the heavy burden of unemployment, which is not due to the municipalities but to the carelessness of this administration which did not find the necessary markets for our production surpluses, with the result that we are overstocked with products of all kinds. Manufacturers are forced to idleness at least a few days a week, due to the fact that they cannot sell their surplus production.

That is what the federal government should have done, besides bringing down legislation such as the one now before us and which we support. But it should also have attended to the immediate situation. If it had followed our suggestions a year or two ago, when we warned the government that there was danger
Vocational Training

ahead and we submitted at least 25 suggestions for new legislation; if it had heeded the suggestions made by the opposition we would probably not be in such a predicament at this time. Unfortunately, the minister claimed at the time that the problem was just temporary. He was listening to advice from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) who was satisfied that the recession was over and that we were on our way to prosperity.

Well, Mr. Chairman, we find today that the advice of the Minister of Finance was based on nothing but his own intuition and that we are now faced with a much more serious situation. If the government has decided to offer effective legislation, I submit that that legislation should be amended in order to be of greater assistance to the younger generation.
I would also ask the government to try and find means to help the needy at this time.

It should not be forgotten, Mr. Chairman, that communism does not thrive on people's prosperity, but on their distress. If these hard times were to continue, people of good will will be seen throwing overboard old principles that they used to hold dear and give themselves to the highest bidder.
The government has some responsibilities, and it should find the ways and means to relieve the present want while getting ready to give assistance to those who tomorrow will have to change jobs.

In view of these facts and the present needs and in the light of this bill, I would ask all members, and especially the Conservative members, to abstain from anything that might delay their own bill so that it can be put into force as soon as possible in order that we may bring forward as soon as possible, bills meant to cope immediately with this unemployment situation which is affecting our population. Thus shall we contribute to the greatest happiness of all, and the Liberal party will readily support this resolution.
(Text):

,Liberal,,Alexis Pierre Caron,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=3c7abf33-5a24-4c46-87e9-5a6c9d457af5&Language=E&Section=ALL
2080626,ca.proc.d.1960-12-02.39.1.3,1960-12-02,9b3d80e9-bd09-42be-a80f-3ac040e3c940,ca.m.8466,Mr. Best:,,VOCATIONAL TRAINING,PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL PROGRAMS,,Mr. Chairman, I am delighted to rise in support of this most important long range measure. I have listened with interest, as I am sure others have, to the hon. member for Hull. We have no difficulty whatsoever, of course, in hearing him. His voice carries very well. However, I did have difficulty in understanding just what he said and what relation it had to the present measure. He discussed many other subjects.

I feel that the measure now before us could have tremendously beneficial effects on unemployment, on industrial manpower and on productivity in Canada in the near future and, indeed, over the long range years ahead. I can think of few measures more vital and more contributory to advancement within our country. There are a number of important problems facing us today and with the changes in technology in our present world and the ever-narrowing horizons of our world today, trained manpower and skilled people are of paramount importance to our country.

When one studies the figures one notices that in the ranks of the unemployed today there are people who in many instances are not specifically trained in a particular skill so as to be able to fill certain positions. In his speech, as found in Hansard of November 25, pages 231 and 232, the Minister of Labour remarked in the ranks of the unemployed the unskilled are approximately three times as numerous as unemployed workers who have specific training or skills. I think this is indicative of the problem before us and the government is taking steps to bring about increased assistance in this regard.

We realize that education in general comes within the sphere of provincial action but in collaboration with the provinces I am sure that the government can advance at present and even more so in the future, the important cause of technical education in our country. Many people have come to Canada in the last 15 years, as a matter of fact somewhere in the neighbourhood of two million, I believe, and we have tried in most instances to bring to Canada those with specific skills who could contribute something to agricultural and industrial production and other important projects within our country. We sometimes see, and this is the unhappy thing, that it is our native born Canadians who are unemployed and who, because of lack of specific training and knowlege to enable them to be fitted into our increasingly complex industrial situation, sometimes cannot avail themselves of the jobs that are open and waiting.

The minister pointed out in his speech, to which I referred earlier, that while there may be numbers of unemployed there are jobs without job-takers in various areas because of a lack of people in the particular area who are specifically trained. I think one of our problems in this regard is perhaps a psychological one that our country will have to face in the present circumstances and in future years. I refer to the recognition of the

dignity and importance of technical training for our people. We are conscious of the tremendous increase in high school and university education and in the need for plant and other facilities, and more teachers and professors, but we must also realize that with the increasing raising of standards in university education and the increasing volume of enrolment not all of our children can make the best and wisest use of that sort of training. In other words, technical training at some level of secondary education in the high schools and, indeed, at the age level of university education, may be a much wiser course for many young people who are coming of age, as it were, to follow.

The minister has pointed out the interesting fact that in the next five years, I presume up to 1965, more than half a million young Canadians will enter the labour market. This very large number of young people coming forward for education and training must in my opinion have in front of them an increased scope for learning and acquiring the skills which are so highly necessary in this day and age. It is because of this that I feel that a long range attack on the sort of technological unemployment that we see in Canada today must be made through constructive measures of this sort.

In a field such as the construction industry and in home building which our government has aided so much in the last three years, we know that as the rise and fall of home building-the flow as it were in this industry -goes, so does a considerable amount of employment or unemployment in various areas. That result is natural. But sometimes these people are unable through lack of skills, when home building has caught up in certain areas, as it has to some extent at least, to fit into other jobs through lack of specific technical training.

I should like to comment on some other remarks made by the minister in this direction. He mentioned the fact that there are large numbers of men and women unemployed for lack of essential skills. He has mentioned and I have quoted the fact that as to the untrained jobless, as it were, the ranks of the unemployed are swelled by these people to a much larger extent. I think we should be truly troubled by these figures. I thought it of great interest to note on page 233 of Hansard the minister's figures indicating that some 5 per cent of all young people enrolled in our secondary schools are taking a technical course program and that of post-high school technical students in Canada-as I presume this figure means- some 8,000 are enrolled in straight technical schools or programs apart from our high
Vocational Training

schools. These figures are really low. They are fantastically low in a country like Canada, a country such as we have here with a small ribbon-like population stretched over a great area, and which must depend now and in the future on our competitive ability to do things better and in a more productive fashion in order to compete with other markets and with other countries around the world which have a longer tradition in technical training and a much larger labour pool.

This measure, of course, ties in as well with the most interesting mention and presentation of a productivity council for Canada, for technical training is closely allied to increased productivity and greater efficiency of industry, agriculture and production of all sorts within our country. I am sure this productivity council will want to work closely in the future with any system or systems of technical education on a municipal, provincial or federal level. These are some of the things which we are examining today.

We have brought to Canada people from many other lands. The minister has pointed out in the past that these countries, of course, have certain differences in programs. They are older countries with longer traditions and perhaps smaller areas and a growth that has been more stable over a longer period of years but not so dynamic as is ours. These countries have the institutions and the facilities with which to train their young people and indeed to train their unemployed for the minister has mentioned that as well as the young people themselves, we must put into effect some scheme or some program by means of which to train and, as it were, almost to rehabilitate for increased usefulness in society some of those who at the present time do not have jobs and positions. The over-all effect of this program I am certain will be of the utmost importance in the years ahead.

As Canada grows and as our population enlarges and as the course of technical progress increases, not decreases-for I am sure it is increasing-this problem of unemployment, this problem of workers fitting into specific positions will enlarge. Our young people and our people of all ages must, if possible, have more basic technical training in order to enable them to have a flexibility to shift from one job to another. On the job training, while useful and while most important, in many instances must be backed by a basic training in a variety of technical fields that can be applied to a variety and wide spectrum of jobs. As technical progress continues I am sure that the sort of move proposed here today will be of most fundamental importance in solving our unemployment problem in Canada and indeed in the
Vocational Training
positive sense aiding in increasing the productivity, the usefulness and the happiness throughout the whole of our land.

2080627,ca.proc.d.1960-12-02.39.1.4,1960-12-02,b815a117-7953-4900-b152-afc56dfc44a1,ca.m.5560,Mr. Herridge:,,VOCATIONAL TRAINING,PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL PROGRAMS,,Mr. Chairman, I rise on behalf of this group to express our support for the purpose and principle of this resolution. However, in doing that, may I say that we are looking forward to seeing the details of the bill in order to make certain that the legislation is comprehensive enough to meet a great and growing need with respect to the technical education of our young people in this country.

I want to place before the committee a few of my opinions with respect to this resolution. I would not for a moment attempt to compete with the dynamic, expansive, impulsive and propulsive hon. member for Hull. However, I am going to utilize my meagre talents in this field in order to give the committee my opinion with respect to this measure.

It is an important measure having regard to the fact that what we do in this field will have a great effect upon the future of hundreds of thousands of young Canadians. There are great possibilities for the development of human character and human happiness and for the promotion of human usefulness in the proper application of the legislation suggested by this resolution. As mentioned by the hon. member who spoke previously, there is a phenomenon that is being noticed more and more across the country, namely the growing percentage of unskilled workers in Canada who are unable to obtain employment. I notice it in my own district, and I am sure it is very general indeed. Also being noticed is the increasing number of boys and girls leaving school who do not go beyond grade eight. When that happens I say there is something wrong with our school curriculums when children are not attracted and inspired in the first instance to continue on with their senior education. Then in other instances there is not the native ability or the desire to follow an academic form of education.

When I say that, may I say that I have had some experience with schools, having been chairman of a school board for a good many years and having had to work with teachers on problems related to the administration of schools. It is a fact that increasing numbers of young people are leaving school on arriving at grade eight or less and are not going on to senior education. If we make ample allowance for those who are not naturally inclined or have not the capacity to go on with academic education, there is something wrong when that situation continues to get worse and worse. We have the largest investment, the best equipment and the best

brained teachers we have ever had in Canadian history so far as schools are concerned, on the lower level particularly, as compared to the little red school houses of from 25 years to 50 years ago-well do I remember them- when children walked three miles to school through three feet of snow and were happy to do so. Now they must be taken there in a bus, and we build a gymnasium in the school in order to give them some exercise so their physical condition will be maintained.

However, I mention this because I am very interested in this question. I see so much of the need for training in my own district. I know of young people whose lives are actually being wasted because they lack the training and the opportunity to attain the skills that are necessary in our technological society.

We need electricians; we need men in the construction industry; we need plumbers; we need bricklayers. It would surprise one to find how difficult it is to obtain first-class tradesmen in the rural areas of Canada. It is difficult to obtain a first-class bricklayer, for example, to build1 a chimney or a wall, or things of that sort. It is also difficult to get plumbers in the smaller communities, because tradesmen are not inclined to go to these smaller communities to obtain a living.

There are some opportunities for tradesmen who want to build up small businesses in many of the smaller communities of this country. I say this from my own experience in the southeastern portion of British Columbia. Also, there is a great opportunity for the training of technicians in the forest industry, in highway construction and other types of construction projects being undertaken throughout this country.

In my opinion we are wasting human resources in two ways. First of all we are wasting human resources because they are untrained technically or as tradesmen to do the things that require to be done to satisfactorily perform the services required in connection with the types of employment I have mentioned. Second, we are wasting human resources in this way. I have had some experience with construction; I have had charge of building a good many miles of highways, and bridges through mountains and in rocky country, through a great deal of rock where thousands of yards of rock or earth had to be moved, and with very primitive equipment compared to nowadays. We are wasting human resources in this respect, because I repeatedly see engineers being^ used to perform a job that a good technician or tradesman could properly perform.

The minister was quite correct when he said that European countries have long recognized the formal paths necessary to acquire occupational skills. That is known from European history and the history of the development of technical and trade schools in Great Britain. We have been very laggard in this respect, as indicated by the number

of persons attending technical schools at the present time. If I heard the minister correctly, the figure is 8,000 students attending technical schools at the present time in a country like this where we have a need for hundreds of thousands of technically trained men and tradesmen.

There is a very narrow margin, shall I say, between a technician and a first-class tradesman in many instances. I was also glad to hear that the government intends to continue research into this problem, because it is a serious question.

There are others who are spending some time studying this question. I was very glad to hear recently that the Canadian welfare council, just from the point of view of the welfare of human beings, is undertaking a very careful study of our manpower needs and the need for technical training, and intends to make representations to the committee of the other place. Also I saw in a press dispatch of November 30 that an interesting representation was made to the committee of the other place by the columnist Mr. F. T. Denton of Toronto. This was an analysis of employment and unemployment in Canada during the past ten years. He said in that report:

Young persons, the unskilled and the less educated are providing Canada with its hard core of unemployment. And if the current trend continues, one million new jobs will be needed in the next five years to absorb the flow of new workers and cut existing unemployment levels to half.
These are pretty startling figures when we are dealing with a problem like this, and I am very pleased to see that there is a growing interest and concern with this question.

The minister mentioned that this system of technical and trade schools was much more advanced in European countries, which is quite correct. I sent to the library for a few books and pamphlets on this question, and I have here a pamphlet issued by the central office of information, reference division, entitled Technological Education in Britain. It is rather interesting. It indicates the possibilities for us. We are only starting in this field in Canada.

I note here that technical education and training first commenced in Great Britain about 1824, as a result of a similar situation to that which is happening in Canada at the present time, but on a much minor scale there. The system progressed very slowly indeed; the tempo of technical education did not really accelerate until the latter part of the Victorian era.
However, to indicate the opportunities which are set out in this pamphlet, there is

the national college of horology and instrument technology, the national foundry college-a college for foundry workers-the national college for heating, ventilating, refrigeration and fan engineering, the national college of rubber technology, the national leathersellers' college, the national college of food technology, the Scottish woollen technical college, and many others. I just mention those to illustrate the possibilities there are for the development of technical schools to provide training in the skills so badly needed in this country.

I am interested in this problem because first of all it is a Canadian problem. It is a widespread and urgent Canadian problem. I am also very interested in the problem because it is of serious concern to my constituents. Because it is a growing problem, school boards in our province have been urging the provincial government to take advantage of the grants that can be obtained from the federal government under the present vocational training act.

We have had vocational training in schools for years. In my opinion, while it is very satisfactory for, shall I say, the elementary teaching of certain trades and abilities and the acquisition of manual skills, and so on, you cannot train technical personnel and tradesmen along with high school students. Success will require a separate school system entirely where young people who have left high school can enter to be trained as technicians or tradesmen.

That is where the whole scheme has to be well planned by the provinces. I understand that under this legislation the initiative will have to come from the provinces. I hope they respond to this legislation and that it will not be a hit-or-miss affair on their part. Surely, our government in British Columbia, with its knowledge of the population and industrial development in the province together with its projection as to the development which can be expected for some years in the future, can plan a system of technical and trade schools to meet the needs of the young people who require training. I trust it will exercise its initiative and co-operate with the federal government in making the legislation envisaged by this resolution a success. This is important to my constituents.

In many cases people who are desirous of attending training schools or technical schools have been denied that opportunity because of the distances which they would have to travel or, often, because of the cost. These schools will have to be fairly close to the persons they are intended to serve and I suggest that in addition to schools to serve

Vancouver island and the main coastal area we shall need establishments to serve southeastern and central British Columbia.

2080634,ca.proc.d.1960-12-02.40.6,1960-12-02,00163189-b2e2-4300-9100-81f7d68a7930,ca.m.4256,Mr. Horner (Acadia):,,I960,,,I think this is a well worth-while measure. Any measure which encourages technical and vocational training is certainly worth supporting, and this ties in nicely with all the other good measures referred to in the speech from the throne. I, too, would like to see this bill brought in as soon as possible, but before that time I should like to suggest a few thoughts which I hope may be reflected in the measure when it is enacted.

With automation advancing at a very fast pace in this highly mechanized North American continent, I think there is a great need for increased technical and vocational training. I am in agreement with the hon. member for Kootenay West that technical and vocational training should be on a higher level than the standard at which it is taught in high schools. I think a person graduating from a vocational or technical school should be able to come out with a degree which will qualify him as a person who has real ability in the field he has chosen to take up.

The province of Alberta from which I come is fast developing into a manufacturing province. Its population is growing rapidly and it is now, I think, the fourth largest province in Canada as far as population is concerned. Because of the success of the oil and gas industry in that province, manufacturing has come to play a prominent part in its development.

Along with the hon. member for Kootenay West, I believe there is a growing need for trained workers. A figure which is not often talked about shows that three out of four jobs becoming available today require a person with a higher education or skill in some trade. This is particularly evident in the province of Alberta as well as in Canada in general. In some of the older countries, particularly in Europe, greater stress is perhaps placed upon sending a person out into the world with a skill or trade of some kind at his disposal. For centuries people grew up in the older countries of the world and, instead of just continuing in school, branched out in the field or skill in which they were trained so as to better equip themselves to compete. Certainly, there are any number of trades which a person can take up-plumbing, electric wiring or electronics, for example. Then, under vocational training, there is a need for butchers and other such trades.

I was interested to hear the hon. member for Kootenay West say there was a great need in some of the rural areas for plumbers and electricians. Men could easily earn a living by going out into some of these rural areas and, possibly, many will be ready to do so after the schools have been set up. I know that in my own constituency, which is largely a rural constituency, there is always a need for plumbers or electricians, whose skills seem to be in high demand. Even in the field of agriculture, with which I am closely connected, there is a growing need for persons with some degree of skill and, in some instances, a high degree of skill. Many advances have been made in the past few years and now we find a large number of farms highly dieselized and highly mechanized, so much so that a farmer has to be a jack of all trades and know a lot about a great number of things if he is to succeed.

In Alberta we have several schools of agriculture, and I graduated from one of them, but I have always thought they could go on and teach highly technical skills in those schools rather than deal in the generalities which some of the subjects cover. They should perhaps give greater training in motor mechanics. Dieselization on the farms has increased the need for this training. Hydraulics today play an important part on the farm. Many farmers find that they require

some knowledge of the subject in order to fit their equipment with hydraulic appliances and measures that will make farming easier and more economical for them.

Together with more stress on motor mechanics greater emphasis should be placed on meat preparation, butchering and other courses relating to animal husbandry. I was pleased to note that the veterinary college in Ontario has an extensive course relating to various types of meat. Certainly this training would better equip a person who was going into butchering or even someone who planned to engage in raising livestock. This too has become highly competitive and highly technical with the implementation of hormones into the feeding rations of livestock. If more extensive teaching were done in relation to these subjects students leaving agricultural colleges or vocational schools would be better equipped to get along in their respective fields.

As an hon. member from Alberta I hope that my home province will be able to take advantage of these grants thereby better preparing the young people to compete and enjoy life in the years ahead.

2080635,ca.proc.d.1960-12-02.40.7,1960-12-02,57dd42c2-427c-4252-9a45-f0c416cc0e1b,ca.m.5944,Mr. Pitman:,,I960,,,Mr. Chairman, as a new member I hesitate to inflict myself on the committee twice in one day but I did want to congratulate the Minister of Labour on bringing this resolution before the committee and to express my earnest hope that it will be introduced as legislation in the very near future.

I rise on this question because I am particularly interested in the area of education. Until only four or five weeks ago I was taking part in education on a full-time scale in another place. Possibly some hon. members would prefer it if I were still doing so.

If this measure is to come up to the expectations of the people of Canada and merit the congratulations of those who sit in this corner of the chamber I think it must fulfil four very important requirements. It must be a dynamic and all-inclusive attempt to meet the needs of every community in these two areas, the training of the unemployed and the training of our young people to meet the demands of this new technological age.
Vocational Training

Second, this proposed legislation surely must be completely adaptable to every community in this nation so that every community will be able to apply to a provincial legislature and take advantage of this measure.
Third, I hope this will be a first step toward a whole new concept of the responsibility of the federal government in the education and training of our youth.
Finally, I hope this will be a part of a new approach to our whole economy for if this proposed legislation is to be effective it must relate itself to a planned, integrated economy.

Unfortunately in the past the whole program of training the unemployed has been most inadequate. Reference has already been made to the Vocational Training Co-Ordination Act passed in 1952 and amended in 1954. As originally envisaged the act was to enable the minister to undertake projects to provide vocational training to fit unemployed persons for gainful employment. In 1954 it was amended to include a provision designed to fit persons for employment for any purpose in the national interest within the legislative authority of the parliament of Canada and approved by the governor in council.

I am not blaming the federal government for the inadequate situation that has obtained in this respect. As I understand it, in many cases the provinces did not even take advantage of the grants that were available. However, across Canada between April, 1958 and March, 1959 there were only 3,568 people trained. I think there were more unemployed in my own constituency last winter than were trained under this program in the whole of Canada. Federal assistance applied for by the provinces in this respect amounted to only $510,479.99.

In a country in which unemployment is a very serious problem surely that is not the scale on which this problem must be met. In Ontario, between April, 1958 and March 31, 1959 there were 94 men and 32 women who were re-trained. I suggest that this problem will not be solved on that scale. The report of the director of Canadian vocational training indicated that the number asking for assistance was not as large as expected. And yet what was the need?

A pamphlet put out by the Department of Labour on the training of skilled manpower admitted that training facilities in Canada were failing to keep pace with the requirement for manpower and that we were importing skilled labour from the United Kingdom and Europe. A winter research program was undertaken to discover the level of ability and training in several areas. It was found, for example, in relation to tool and

diemakers that only 8.5 per cent of Canadian tradesmen in this field had received secondary education in appropriate technical training whereas 46 per cent of non-Canadian tool and diemakers had received adequate training in this trade. That is a commentary upon vocational training throughout this nation as it takes place in the provinces.

If this program is to have a sufficient impact to be of any use in the twentieth century it must be undertaken on a scale that will make everything we have done before look absolutely ridiculous. It is significant that in my own riding of Peterborough we have a general union of unemployed workers. I hope this union will not grow very much stronger but if the situation worsens it may well become the largest union in the riding.

These men have done more than whine about their situation. They are in a serious plight. While perhaps they are not dropping in the streets they are nevertheless suffering mentally and spiritually. Rather than whine about their plight they have taken positive steps through every level of government to provide this kind of training for their members through the hard winter. It is only through re-training that the unemployed will solve their problems when they feel that once again they can make a useful contribution to the community where they live. It is not a matter of accepting a dole. They do not want unemployment insurance. What they want is to return, so to speak, to Canadian society in a useful, vital capacity. I hope this resolution will help these people.

It is important that this program be adaptable to each community. Technical institutions cannot be built in some communities which are too small to support them. I hope this resolution will provide grants whereby these areas may perhaps use the money to provide for their unemployed transportation to some other centre where there is a technical institution that can provide the type of training these people need. I hope it will provide grants not just for buildings but for areas which have buildings which may be used. I suggest vocational schools which might be used from four o'clock in the afternoon until seven or eight o'clock at night. I hope it may possibly provide money for teaching and also for the maintenance of equipment in a great many areas where people could be trained adequately and on the basis of what is possible in the community in which those unemployed people live. It is possible that there will be need to provide assistance to men so that they can take those courses and not mean a hardship to their wives and families when they are actually taking part
in the course. I hope that the legislation will be not only dynamic and all-inclusive, but that it will also be adaptable.

I hope it will provide a new motivation for vocational training. I think that unfortunately we in Canada have never come to acquire the kind of feeling which people in European countries and the United Kingdom have for their crafts. I think we need to motivate people in the direction of vocational training, and instil in them a pride in vocational training. Too often vocational training has become a kind of second rate education. It has been suggested that a vocational school is a dumping ground for the less gifted. I think this has brought vocational training into disrepute in many communities of this nation. I hope that through this legislation vocational training will reach new heights of acceptability by the people of the provinces of this country.

I think we desperately need technicians. We must forget the idea that a technician is a second grade engineer, or an engineer that did not make good. As the hon. member suggested, too often we have people with engineering degrees doing jobs which could be done by technicians. This is an area where the Soviet union has completely surpassed us in education. This is an area where we must catch up. Particularly I hope that this is going to be a step toward a whole new concept as to what the federal government must do through grants, not to control all education but without endangering the autonomy of the provinces to provide assistance to education and training on a scale that will allow every person in this country to attain the height of achievement of which he is capable.

It has been suggested by the dominion bureau of statistics that over the next number of years we will need ten major universities in this country, not all centred in the larger communities but some also in smaller communities. I think one of the unfortunate aspects is that our university education is centred in the large metropolitan areas. In an area like my own, Peterborough, we have people who are desperately trying to set up a junior college. They need help.

This is also a whole new step toward the opening up of a whole new vista of federal assistance and motivation in the area of education because if we wish to make our educational system as good as it must be in the latter part of the twentieth century we need not only technicians and craftsmen but also economists, historians, philosophers and theologians. We need these as well. Let us not provide technicians and discover that the whole meaning of our western civilization has

disappeared because we forgot that vocational training was only a part of our educational process.
Finally, it must be integrated somehow into a planned economy, and here again I hope, as the hon. member suggested, that the productivity council will come into play.

I thought when listening to the hon. member that what he gave us really sounded just like a schoolteacher's definition. However, now that we have this new party definition we can have both free enterprise and socialism together. Unfortunately, this is not true. This is just the socialist's way of gaining power, and then the rest of the restrictions of individual freedom have to come into play, because this is the only way the socialists can operate a planned economy, by having complete stat-ism, and it does not really matter very much whether you call it socialism, communism, or anything else. It means a complete lack of individual freedom and, as such, no longer do we have a free world or a free country.

I suggest to the hon. member that this measure is brought forward not as a part of a planned economy but as a plan on the part of a dynamic government to provide opportunity for all Canadians. So far as I am concerned, there are a few points I should like to touch on briefly. They have been touched on by a previous speaker, but I should like to bring to your attention, sir, the question of decentralization of the schools.

In my area in Alberta particularly, we are concerned and have been concerned not about the importation of European skilled workers but of United States skilled workers in the oil and gas and the pipe line industries. We are now on the verge of terrific expansion in our area with regard to natural gas and the processing plants and extraction plants that go along with it. Very recently I visited one in the Pembina field at the town of Drayton Valley and talked to the young people there who are running these plants. All of them were studying by correspondence and were receiving on the job training under supervision. This was one of the first plants in operation in Alberta and we have several others. We have another one in the Jumping Pound field in southern Alberta and construction is just going to start on another one in the Windfall field in my constituency. There will be a series of these gas extraction and processing plants throughout Alberta.
We are concerned about these plants being manned by United States technicians because

we do not have trained personnel in Canada. I should like to put it on the record that I hope the province of Alberta will take advantage of this program to establish immediately a technical school devoted to the oil and gas industry. In that regard I suggest to them that the town of Drayton Valley would be an ideal location for such a school as it offers all the on the job training required and is centrally located among the major gas and oil fields in the province.

I wish to put another point on the record with regard to the question of decentralization and I should like to quote from the report of the Cameron royal commission on education in the province of Alberta. In this regard they came to this conclusion:
That the scope of educational offerings at public expense in the public school system be broadened to include appropriate courses in many vocational areas.

They went on to suggest that this should be done by a program that would promote and develop community colleges specializing in the particular line which had to do with the raw materials or natural resources of the area. This is why I bring up the question of the oil and gas industry and a technical school in the town of Drayton Valley which is in the centre of the largest oil field in North America.

I wish to refer to one or two other aspects of vocational training and I should like to deal first with forestry. The provincial government recently established a school of forestry at Hinton which so far is under the direction of the department of lands and forests of the province. However, I hope they will see fit to convert it into an educational institution devoted to producing technicians for the forest industry, an institution which would serve northwestern Alberta and part of British Columbia as well.

There is another matter in which I have been interested for a great number of years as a result of my experience many years ago when I served on a town council. From what I can observe there is a great need right across Canada for trained municipal, town and city officials, employees with some training in municipal, provincial and federal law and with some elementary training in bookkeeping. I suggest to the authorities that this might be a field for the establishment of a technical school devoted to the training of municipal officials. In my view it would be a real step forward from the point of view of providing jobs and also providing improved and more efficient administration of our municipalities, towns and cities.
There is one other question I want to raise and it is one I have brought up before in the house on numerous occasions. It has to

do with veterinary medicine. We in western Canada are still hopefully waiting for a school of veterinary medicine. I suggest that perhaps the province could tie in with such a school a program of technical training to produce the technicians required in veterinary medicine and all other aspects of animal husbandry.

Although I realize this may be a provincial responsibility, I believe that if we are going to remain free we have to do more than just provide a technical education for our people, and in this regard I should like to quote from the Cameron commission minority report:

A school that furnishes only a narrow, vocational, workaday training to children of humble parentage is effectually denying the innate dignity of man, a doctrine which asserts that every individual, whatever his trade or his income, is entitled to share in the high, humane tradition of the liberal arts and sciences.

This latter is I think an effective answer to the speech of the hon. member for Peterborough. Most of what he had to say was good until he started to talk about a planned economy and the area in which he would have the government take control. The fallacy of the thinking of the socialists or the new party, if their new program is one of half free enterprise and half socialism, is that these things cannot work together any more than they can take one section of the public, as they are trying to do by taking the labouring class, and make a political party out of them for the purposes, I suspect, of the people who are directing the labour unions rather than for the good of the ordinary working man.

2080642,ca.proc.d.1960-12-02.40.14,1960-12-02,5322cf37-a057-49f9-b020-3806cf282371,ca.m.2822,Mr. Kindt:,,I960,,,Mr. Chairman, I want to thank the Minister of Labour for having introduced this resolution on technical and vocational training. I am particularly interested to learn from the resolution the broad scope and intention of the government. The resolution seeks to authorize the Minister of Labour to enter into agreements with provincial governments for the encouragement of technical and vocational training and to authorize the making of contributions by Canada toward the cost of the training programs undertaken under provincial authority, including contributions toward the cost of capital expenditures on training facilities connected with such programs.

First of all, I think the important point is that this work is going to be carried on in co-operation with the provinces under agreements with them. Each province will be approached and the plans will be worked out. Undoubtedly the plans may vary to a certain extent from province to province. I shall be extremely interested along with the
Vocational Training
people of southwestern Alberta, whom I represent, in the agreement which is to be worked out with the province of Alberta.
I also note from the text of the resolution that technical and vocational training are to be undertaken under provincial authority.
It is well for us to note that all training which is undertaken will be under the authority of the province which has jurisdiction over education.

The resolution goes on to state that the purpose is to authorize the Minister of Labour to undertake programs of technical and vocational training for specified categories of persons, to provide for the establishment and operation of an advisory council and the appointment of the members and staff and to define its duties, and to provide for other related and incidental matters. The point of great importance there is that technical and vocational training programs are to be undertaken for specified categories and that raises a question in my mind as to what categories will receive vocational and technical training.

All who have spoken on this resolution seem to be agreed that know-how is necessary. They did not use exactly that term but I do so. I believe that any person wishing to make his way in this world must first of all prepare himself with some specialized know-how by means of which to handle a particular job. Whether it is a matter of working with his hands or of working with his brain he must be trained and he must have the skill with which to handle the work he is undertaking.

To come to the vocational end, may I say this. It has been mentioned by others that we should have more people who are able to do such jobs as carpentering-or at least have more training in that field-people able to read blueprints, to do plumbing work, bricklaying, electrical work, stonecutting, blacksmithing and electric welding, etc. Whether you call these people technicians or tradesmen is immaterial for my purposes. It is not necessary for me to distinguish between them, although there is a slight difference. What I am saying is that training for these various trades is work that would be handled in a technical and vocational training school.

The great need for training in these fields requires no extra words on my part or on the part of anyone else. One only needs to try to hire somebody to do any of these specialized jobs in order to find that those available are not as plentiful as they might be.
There is another point that I should like to make and it is on the matter of who should receive this technical and vocational training. I hope the resolution which refers to
Vocational Training

specified categories of persons will include young farmers and young city dwellers. There should be some provision for night classes for students of all ages. Above all, I think these training institutions should provide for technical and vocational training to Indians. There is on Indian reserves a small group of students who could be sent to these technical schools. They might not consist of any more than 5 per cent of the total enrollment at a school but they would benefit greatly from technical and vocational training.

I was on the Eden Valley Indian reserve last fall and the need for vocational training among these Indians was forcibly brought to my attention. If they were even able to take a hammer and saw, go out and cut down a few trees and shape them into homes, it would be of great assistance. It is a rather simple operation. It was performed even by our forefathers in pioneer days but it seems as though it has not been one of those skills which the Indian has acquired. If he were given this vocational training he would be able to provide for himself, not only a decent home but would be able to raise his standard of living.

I have given considerable thought to the question of technical and vocational training schools. Some two years ago I tried my best to get the provincial government of Alberta to start one of those schools at Claresholm and to take advantage of the splendid facilities of the R.C.A.F. field which is at that centre. I should like to say that some consideration was given to the suggestion. Under this resolution and federal program financial assistance is to be given by the federal government and an arrangement is to be worked out with the province of Alberta and I suggest that every consideration be given to the R.C.A.F. station at Claresholm as a suitable site for a new technical and vocational training school.

In closing I want to say again that this is far-reaching legislation and should benefit all classes in our society. Above all, I want to compliment the Minister of Labour once more on bringing in this resolution which is designed to assist in encouraging technical and vocational training throughout all of Canada.

2080651,ca.proc.d.1960-12-02.41.1.1,1960-12-02,ba1f4916-0b63-4654-9f27-242c3d276e6e,ca.m.6904,Mr. Frank Howard (Skeena) moved,,CANADA FAIR EMPLOYMENT PRACTICES ACT,AMENDMENT TO EXTEND APPLICATION TO CIVIL SERVICE,,the second reading of Bill No. C-9, to amend the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act (crown bound).

He said: Mr. Speaker, my remarks on the introduction of this particular bill will be quite few, because the contents of it are rather short and need no extensive introduction. I think the proposed principle is clear and well established. Also, we had a debate lasting an hour on a bill of a similar nature during the last session.

Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, I should say this. The Canada Fair Employment Practices Act which came into force in the summer of 1953-in July, I believe it was-contains the provision, in brief form, that an employer shall not discriminate against employees or potential employees in so far as race, national origin, colour or religion is concerned. It also provides that a trade union shall not

discriminate against potential or present members, nor shall it expel members on the ground or for the reason of race, national origin, colour or religion. The act also sets out certain procedures for the enforcement of its provisions and certain penalties if the act is contravened. Those parts are not germane to this particular bill but are only by way of an aside in this introduction.

We know it is not possible to legislate for a state of mind. Yet it is good to have on the statute books something of this nature that is an anti-discrimination statute, that protects individuals from discrimination because of race, colour, national origin, and so on. It tends to promote the cessation or the lessening of any acts of discrimination that may be based upon those factors that I mentioned earlier.

Perhaps I may read very briefly from section 3 of the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act-which this bill seeks to amend- in order that hon. members should understand how this act applies now. Section 3 reads:

This act applies to and in respect of employment upon or in connection with any work, undertaking or business that is within the legislative authority of the parliament of Canada, including, but not so as to restrict the generality of the foregoing-

Then it sets out a number of things to which it applies. Section 3 (m) is the relevant passage to which I wish to refer, namely: the employment by any corporation established to perform any function or duty on behalf of the government of Canada of employees.

This means that Canadian National Railways, T.C.A., the atomic energy commission, Polymer and the like are covered by this particular act and shall not engage in any of the practices that the present act prohibits.

The purpose of the bill before us is to extend the application of the provisions of the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act to the crown and to the employees of the crown; or, in effect, Her Majesty in right of Canada and the servants and agents of Her Majesty in right of Canada.

One of the principles behind proposing this bill, from our point of view, is that employees in the public service of Canada should be treated substantially the same as employees in private industry in Canada. By that I do not wish to imply that they should be treated as they have been within the last few days by this parliament because of the bill with which we have just dealt. But in general terms they should come into the same set of legislative provisions and regulations in so far as employee-employer relationships are concerned.
I am quite sure, and there is no shadow of a doubt in my mind-and I am sure there
Vocational Training

is no shadow of a doubt in the mind of anyone in this house-that the intent of the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act is followed by the civil service commission in its function of employing people. I am also quite sure that no discrimination exists on these bases whatsoever.

We had some discussion last session. A number of hon. members participated in the debate and raised a number of questions. Perhaps I might briefly deal with those questions at this time. One question raised was whether there might be an inconsistency in applying the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act to the provisions of the Civil Service Act or the regulations made thereunder.

Last year I undertook to check by telephone-and again this year I undertook to check by telephone-with the civil service commission to ascertain whether there existed in the Civil Service Act or in any of the regulations pursuant to it any reference to non-discrimination. I was told that there was no such reference in the act or regulations at the moment. I inquired further and was told that in 1942 there appeared on one of the old employment questionnaires to be completed by potential employees a reference to the colour of the individual, but that this did not now exist.

I was unable to determine just when the transitional point took place, when the reference to colour was eliminated from the questionnaires. I was told that it had existed in 1942 but does not exist at the moment and has not for some time.

I expect this year, if last session's activities are to be followed through, we will be having committees and we will have presented, I presume, a revised civil service bill. I assume that at the behest of the government it will be referred to a special committee of the house. Perhaps it would be appropriate this year for this particular bill now before us to receive endorsation and second reading, because I am certain that every hon. member supports the basic principle behind it. I think the bill should receive second reading at this stage and be referred to this special committee in order that the committee can study the Civil Service Act and the proposed changes thereto. The committee will be able to intermesh, if it so desires, or interweave the principle of this bill into the structure of that act, by either reporting this bill in a favourable light or by intermeshing it into the provisions of the Civil Service Act.
In that way parliament will decide that the act which applies to all other employees in Canada under our national jurisdiction
Vocational Training

shall also apply to the crown in its employment policies. I say again that this is in no way implying that such discrimination exists at the moment, or that such discrimination has existed before. To my knowledge no such discrimination has existed until today except, as I am told, by the reference to colour on the civil service questionnaire.

Whether this actually constitutes discrimination or not is another matter. I think that perhaps those few words will suffice. I am looking forward to perhaps a more pleasant discussion on this particular bill than we have had in the past few days. Also, perhaps there will be less opportunity to resort to questions of privilege on this bill than there was on the bill with which we have just dealt.

2080654,ca.proc.d.1960-12-02.41.1.4,1960-12-02,e61bd809-11ad-4416-a3a1-72e6c1dcfddc,ca.m.5387,Mr. Broome:,,CANADA FAIR EMPLOYMENT PRACTICES ACT,AMENDMENT TO EXTEND APPLICATION TO CIVIL SERVICE,,That is rather a short bill which really is not going to change anything as things are today, because the civil service commission, according to his own words, does not practice discrimination in any form in the selection or treatment of its employees. In fact, the hon. member for Skeena underlined this last session, because when introducing his bill he said, as reported on page 1271 of Hansard for February 19, 1960:

The bill which is before the house at the moment is very short. It merely seeks to make the present Canada Fair Employment Practices Act applicable to Her Majesty, her servants, and agents of Her Majesty, or, in effect, applicable to the civil service and to employees in the government service. This, of course, does not suggest that with regard to the employment of civil servants there exists at the present time any such discrimination because of the factors that I set out earlier. In fact, I think I can say without any contradiction or any qualification that no such discrimination enters into the employment of candidates for the civil service.

That is a very straightforward statement and, I believe, a true statement. An equally true statement, which the hon. member for Skeena has just made, is that it is not possible to legislate for a state of mind. It may

be that in practice he and his colleagues do not always follow that axiom, but it is nevertheless true that you cannot legislate into being characteristics which will eliminate intolerance and discrimination. In order to solve this problem we must look to education rather than to laws. I believe that while in Canada today we are not free from discrimination we are freer than many other countries and that we are becoming increasingly alive to the fact that intolerance and discrimination are not worthy of a nation such as this. I believe the people of this country are going along that road, but they are travelling in spurts, and there is, as I say, still a measure of intolerance in sections of the country and in groups.
If the hon. member for Skeena was not too happy about the previous bill which we have been discussing he should have been happy about the bill of rights, the preamble to which states as follows:

The parliament of Canada, affirming that the Canadian nation is founded upon principles that acknowledge the supremacy of God, the dignity and worth of the human person and the position of the family in a society of free men and free institutions:
Affirming also that men and institutions remain free only when freedom is founded upon respect for moral and spiritual values and the rule of law;
Certainly intolerance and discrimination are not the spiritual values referred to here. Part I of the Bill of Rights reads as follows:

It is hereby recognized and declared that in Canada there have existed and shall continue to exist without discrimination by reason of race, national origin, colour, religion or sex, the following human rights and fundamental freedoms, namely,
I do not intend to read them all, but I will read the first one:

column2: the right of the individual to life, liberty, security of the person and enjoyment of property, and the right not to be deprived thereof except by due process of law;

column1: I submit that ""liberty"" must include the right of employment. Liberty must include the right to make a livelihood without discrimination based on race, religion, national origin, colour or sex.

The hon. member said he had been checking over the various speeches which were made last year when a similar bill was considered, but I note he failed to cover the point raised by the hon. member for Essex West (Mr. Spencer) who brought out the conflict between this measure and the actual set-up of the civil service commission in that the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act is administered by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) and the civil service of Canada is administered by a civil service commission which is responsible to parliament and to parliament alone. The hon. member for Essex

West, who is I believe a lawyer, went into the details of this conflict, and I will go as far as to read what I suggest to be the conclusion which he reached. I am quoting from page 1274 of Hansard for February 19:

In. other words, the Minister of Labour would then be directing the civil service commission to do something it had not done or undo something it had done which in his opinion of the inquiry commission amounted to discrimination.

The hon. member was referring to the fact that the Minister of Labour under this measure could set up an industrial inquiry commission to hear complaints, and I suggest this would certainly bring two branches of government administration into conflict.

Another point which might be considered is whether veterans' preference is not discrimination to some extent. Yet it has been the instruction of this parliament that there should be a preference shown to veterans in connection with civil service commission hiring. There may be restrictions, and there are restrictions in certain fields where security is the prime consideration. Is this discrimination? Evidently the hon. member does not believe that this sort of thing is discrimination, because he categorically stated that there is no discrimination in the civil service.

column1: If I understand correctly the purpose of this bill it is to extend to those engaged in the civil service of Canada the benefits that are presently enjoyed by people in other walks of life. It is also my understanding that the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act now encompasses the employees of crown corporations but not the employees of the civil service.

This bill appears to anticipate something that will be coming before parliament in the not too distant future. Reference was made by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Broome) to the forthcoming revision of the Civil Service Act. It might be said that the passage of this bill would not in any way change what might take place at a later time in regard to that act that will be considered at a later date but I submit there is a difference-and it may be a shade of a difference-between the ordinary employees in Canada and those employed by the government of this country. That fact is borne out by some of the provisions now contained in the Civil Service Act.

I refer first of all to the preference to veterans, an association of ideas which I believe Canadians in all parts of the country want to see maintained because of the unequalled contribution that has been made to the preservation of the freedom of Canada by those who have served in the Canadian armed forces, a freedom extending not only to these individuals themselves but to Canadians in all walks of life.

Coupled with that premise, of course, is the other premise relating to those provisions incorporated into the Civil Service Act having to do with the problem of security. The problem of ideological warfare-if you want

to call it that-the clash of ideas from one end of the globe to the other certainly makes every one of us here in the House of Commons and I believe everyone in Canada stop to think when he considers some of the positions that must be held by the people in the employ of the government of this country. It may be said that this is discrimination but I think Canadians in general will agree that it is one of the things necessary for the preservation of our way of life and of the sovereignty of this nation.

I notice that this bill was brought forward last year and discussed' in January and February. No doubt hon. members are familiar with the discussion that took place at that particular time. As I read to you, sir, the provisions that this bill would provide I could not help but ask myself the question: Are any of those provisions already provided for Canadians by virtue of the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act and the provisions that were brought forward last year in the bill of rights, that bill which more than any other was so long overdue in this parliament.

When people talk of discrimination they mention, of course, discrimination in so far as race, colour and religion are concerned. Sometimes there are other forms of discrimination as well. Generally speaking, Canada is free from these types of discrimination. In fact, it would be difficult to put your finger in a substantive way on any particular case at any particular time. There have been times in the past, of course, particularly during wartime, when acts of parliament and decisions of the government have made necessary in the ordinary deliberations of parliament the passing of certain statutes which seemed to have caused a certain measure of discrimination; but, generally speaking, in most instances, those acts were passed for the preservation of freedom in this country, and as such were accepted by Canadian citizens in good faith.

Because of the fact that Canada is reasonably free from this type of discrimination, because of the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act as it stands today, because of the bill of rights, because of the examination of the Civil Service Act, which will be brought forward later on in this session, I cannot help but feel that this bill serves no useful purpose at this particular time in our deliberations and for that reason, I thought that I should voice those expressions of opinion so that other hon. members might judge for themselves as well.
