Browne (Vancouver-Kingsway):,,CANADA FAIR EMPLOYMENT PRACTICES ACT,AMENDMENT TO EXTEND APPLICATION TO CIVIL SERVICE,,Mr. Speaker, with the statement that is contained in the explanatory notes of this bill to the effect that the purpose of this bill is

to prevent discrimination by the government of Canada against its employees or applicants for employment in the public service, I think everyone would agree. Of course, if any case was brought forward to substantiate the claim that there was any such discrimination I am sure we would want to take immediate action to prevent it. However, in this particular case the mover of the bill has stated that to his knowledge there is no such discrimination. Of course, that relieves us of the necessity of taking immediate action.

In view of the fact that the civil service is not generally covered in the same legislation as the rest of our labour force and has not been throughout the years, it is obviously a matter that needs a good deal of consideration. The Civil Service Act, of course, has been set up to deal with employees in the public service, and I think it has been generally conceded throughout the years that public servants have responsibilities and conditions different from those of other employees in the country. Many things have been put in the Civil Service Act to protect those employees, and there are certain advantages that they have enjoyed throughout the years that other employees have not had. Therefore, I do not think we can just accept the statement that everybody should be brought under the same legislation.

As has already been pointed out in connection with this bill, if it were passed it would bring the civil servants under the control of two different bodies. It would have the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) responsible for part of their activities and the civil service commission responsible for another part.

As I have already pointed out, with the study being made of the whole position of the civil service I think it would be unwise to make such a change at this time. I think in the Civil Service Act there are ample safeguards at the present time to prevent discrimination in the civil service. In chapter 48 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, section 19, the following appears:

Except where otherwise expressly provided, all appointments to the civil service shall be upon competitive examination under and pursuant to this act, and shall be during pleasure; but no appointment, whether permanent or temporary, shall be made to a local position within a province, and no employee shall be transferred from a position in a province to a local position in the same or in another province, whether permanent or temporary, until and unless the candidate or employee has qualified, by examination,-
Then, in section 25 we find:
(1) Competitive examinations shall be held by the commission to establish lists of persons eligible for appointment.
Vocational Training

(2) Such examinations may be written or oral or in the form of a demonstration of skill or any combination of these, and they shall be of a character fairly to test and determine the relative fitness and ability of candidates actually to perform the duties of the class to which they seek to be appointed, and any investigation of training and experience and any test of technical knowledge, manual skill, or physical fitness that, in the judgment of the commission, serves to this end may be employed.

In that way the examinations are open to everyone, and that in itself provides an adequate guarantee that everybody is going to have a fair opportunity of employment in the civil service. However, as has been pointed out, there are some advantages given for employment in the civil service by way of war veterans' preference. I would not be surprised to see proposed the suggestion that there should be other preference given. My own feeling is that perhaps we should specify that a preference should be given to Canadian citizens. I do not think that that would be an unwarranted preference, and yet under the terms of this proposed amendment it may well be that the power to have people given that preference may be taken out of our hands.

The bill of rights has already been referred to on several occasions, and that is another guarantee that there is going to be fairness in the application of the act. However, I have another reason for believing that the civil service should not some within the scope of the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act, because I believe there are other amendments that need to be made to that act and that perhaps the civil service should not necessarily come within the scope of those kinds of amendments.

For this reason I believe it would be very unwise to proceed with this amendment at this time. I should like to be able to deal with some of the other amendments that I feel should be made to the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act but I fear, Mr. Speaker, that you would rule me out of order at this time so I shall save them for another occasion.

2080671,ca.proc.d.1960-12-02.41.1.21,1960-12-02,eb1f264f-a92e-4bc5-a5da-0ac8c84dbd5c,ca.m.7239,Mr. Maclnnis:,,CANADA FAIR EMPLOYMENT PRACTICES ACT,AMENDMENT TO EXTEND APPLICATION TO CIVIL SERVICE,,Reference has been made to the bill of rights. I should like to point out that discrimination is completely guarded against under the bill of rights because in section 2 it is provided that every law of Canada shall, unless it is expressly declared by an act of the parliament of Canada that it shall operate notwithstanding the Canadian bill of rights, shall be so construed and applied as not to abrogate, etc., any rights or freedoms. Since the Civil Service Act comes under this jurisdiction this offers complete protection against discrimination on the ground of race, colour, creed or nationality.

The bill before us is an act to amend the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act and its chief purpose is to extend the act to bind Her Majesty in right of Canada and servants and agents of Her Majesty in right of Canada. At the present time crown corporations come within the ambit of the act. Section 3 of the act reads as follows:

This act applies to and in respect of employment upon or in connection with any work, undertaking or business that is within the legislative authority of the parliament of Canada, including, but not so as to restrict the generality of the foregoing.. .
(m) the employment by any corporation established to perform any function or duty on behalf of the government of Canada of employees.
That makes the act apply only to employees of Her Majesty in right of Canada.

The civil service commission has always followed a policy of non-discrimination and has never knowingly transgressed the principles laid down in the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act so far as race, colour or religion are concerned. Any differences in

treatment or application which can be attributed to race or origin have been imposed by the requirements of the provisions of the Civil Service Act. The civil service commission has revised its application forms from time to time to delete or modify questions of a nature incompatible with the provisions of the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act as applied to employees in private industry. This was done because of the close, informal working relations between the Department of Labour and the civil service commission with regard to the application of the principles of the act.

The Civil Service Act gives certain preferences to war veterans and residents of a locality in filling jobs in a particular area and also with respect to the admission to examination of British subjects with at least five years residence in Canada. From time to time, however, as the need arises the commission departs from the operation of the relevant section with respect to a position where it is necessary to admit to examination people who do not qualify in these respects.

The provisions of section 4 of the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act have to do with discrimination on the ground of race, colour or religion, and while it may be contended that in the case of British subjects there is special provision, the effect of the amendment would be to give the Minister of Labour authority to deal with complaints concerning discrimination in employment which in all other respects are subject to the Civil Service Act and the administration of the civil service commission. In view of this situation there could not conceivably be any conflict in the exercise of this authority.

The status given by the bill to the Minister of Labour and to the industrial inquiry commission appointed under the act would be repugnant to the Civil Service Commission reporting as it does solely to parliament and not being under the supervision or direction of any minister of the crown. As outlined, the policies and practices of the commission in protecting a person seeking employment or who is already employed in the public service from discrimination on the basis of national origin, colour, creed or religion, are based upon the application of the principles employed in the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act, the Civil Service Act or otherwise.

I know that from time to time the commission has revised its application forms to delete or modify questions of a nature considered incompatible with the provisions of the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act as applied to employers in private industry. I understand that there are provisions in

the Civil Service Act or the regulations made thereunder that are applicable to appointments to the civil service in relation to residence, security, or citizenship which might be inconsistent with the literal application of the amendment to the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act proposed in the bill.

In view of the considerations referred to it might be deemed preferable that the purpose of the bill should be given effect to under the Civil Service Act rather than under the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act. This consideration is particularly pertinent at this time when legislation for the enactment of a new Civil Service Act is projected for the present session of parliament.
